news.title: Are the midterms the beginning of the end of the Trump political project?
news.text:
When Donald Trump won the 2024 US election against Kamala Harris, he pulled together a coalition of voters that don't have much history voting Republican.

Working class and lower income voters helped deliver him key swing states like Pennsylvania, Michigan and Wisconsin, while Hispanic voters helped turn the sun belt states of Arizona and Nevada red.

Research from Pew found that Trump voters were markedly more racially and ethnically diverse in 2024 (20 per cent non-white) than they were in 2020 (14 per cent) and 2016 (10 per cent).

Virtually all demographic groups swung to Trump in 2024, but a New York Times analysis concluded the biggest shifts were among young Black and Hispanic voters.

At the time of that election, strategists wondered if Trump had catalysed a political realignment in the country that would continue to work in Republicans' favour.

But converting irregular voters into reliable members of the Republican base is not easy.

Two years on, as the cost of living bites, they don't appear to have stuck around, and the Hispanic voters that swung behind Trump have either swung right back to the Democrats, or are choosing to sit this election out.

The Republican Party appears almost certain to lose control of the House of Representatives in next week's midterm elections. Democrats also lead in polls in more than enough Senate races to be able to take control of that chamber as well (although many of those leads are within the margin of error).

Among the list of prizes that Democrats are hoping to pick up next week, the state of Texas glistens seductively.

Democrats haven't won a senate seat in the state since 1988, but this year, their candidate James Talarico is leading Republican candidate Ken Paxton in polling.

Republicans appear to be vulnerable in deep red states, and in recent weeks Trump has held rallies on Kansas, Iowa, Oklahoma and Alabama. That is not the strategy of a party that's feeling confident.

Donald Trump isn't on the ballot this year, but at rallies he has repeatedly asked voters to "pretend" he is.

"They say that Trump does great when he's on the ballot, but when he's not on the ballot … his people don't come and they don't vote for senators, congressmen," he said at a rally in South Carolina in August.

Part of the Trump campaign's strategy in 2024 was to increase turnout rates among people who would usually stay home. Among the group of people who voted in that election but not in 2020, Pew estimated Trump had a 12 percentage point lead over Harris.

High turnout helped him two years ago. This year, it may be part of his undoing.

Trump wants voters to be thinking about him when they consider voting, because last time that drove lots of people to the polls.

The trouble is that, in 2026, the president is very unpopular.

Nobody's ever seen a president so disliked

American politicians are, as a general rule, held in much lower regard now than they used to be. But amidst an unpopular bunch, Donald Trump is reaching new depths.

YouGov and the Economist have been regularly tracking views on US presidents by asking voters whether they approve or disapprove of the job the leader is doing.

In his first term, Trump was into net negative territory effectively from the moment he took office. President Biden was in the negatives within seven months.

But in his second term, Trump has plummeted. A week out from polling day, the Economist recorded a net approval rating of -27, with 34 per cent of voters approving of the job he's doing and 61 per cent disapproving.

That is a lower net approval rating than any other president has recorded just before their midterm elections since World War II.

Given the president's party nearly always goes backwards in the House of Representatives, and that the Republicans only need to lose three seats to lose control of the House, it's not hard to see why forecasters are tipping a Democrat win.

If the midterms go as poorly for Republicans as opinion polls suggest, it could threaten Trump's command of the public's attention, as well as his authority over his party.

While he'll be in office for another two years, there's always an election around the corner in the US, and once the midterms are behind us attention will start to shift to the 2028 presidential election.

The results of these midterm elections will be an important moment in defining Trump's political legacy, as candidates start to position themselves for potential runs.

The current president regularly backs his preferred candidates in Republican primaries, and he believes his endorsement carries weight.

But will Republicans in the future be keen to embrace the Trump political project, or will they be keeping their distance the moment he's seen as a lame duck president?
news.summary: Donald Trump wants American voters to "pretend" he's on the ballot these midterm elections. Voters don't need to be reminded how much they dislike him.
news.author: Casey Briggs

news.title: Obama mocks Trump for 'mobilizing whole government' to respond to his Cheesecake Factory joke: 'He was very upset'
news.text:
Obama mocks Trump for ‘mobilizing whole government' to respond to his Cheesecake Factory joke: 'He was very upset'

Sign up HERE to our DC Insider newsletter for your guide on all the latest from the midterms campaign trail and what's rattling the White House 

By ELINA SHIRAZI, US SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER

Published: 01:21 GMT, 29 October 2026 | Updated: 02:03 GMT, 29 October 2026

Former President Barack Obama took the stage in Georgia to campaign for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, with a fresh attack against President Donald Trump.

Obama saved his biggest comedic lines for the White House's reaction to his earlier critiques, escalating a dig where he compared the White House renovations to Saddam Hussein opening a Cheesecake Factory.

'The President wasn't even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison,' Obama observed. 'That part didn't bother him - but he was very upset about the Cheesecake Factory part.'

Obama claimed he 'mobilized' the whole government over the joke, and continued to describe the response from the administration following the remarks.

'The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy, the person who's supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable, the guy who's supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation and reduce interest rates,' Obama said. 

'They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory!'

Obama also made sharp digs at Trump's cabinet secretaries. Specifically, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

'The defense secretary is laser-focused on very important matters like the jawline and testosterone levels of our troops, and live streaming executions because that's how he thinks you cultivate that manly warrior spirit,' Obama remarked.

Opening his critiques, Obama once again poked fun at Trump's extensive remodeling projects at the White House. 

'That guy is building a ballroom that is bigger than the White House. He's paved over the rose garden. Put a helicopter pad on the south lawn, and there is gold everywhere. Take a picture. So much gold,' Obama said to roaring laughter. 

Former President Barack Obama took the stage in Georgia to campaign for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, with a fresh attack against President Donald Trump

Supporters and rally attendees arrive at The Arena at Southlake for the Democratic Party's 'United for Georgia' campaign rally in Morrow, Georgia

The former President's visit aims to rally support for Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is seeking reelection against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running against Republican Rick Jackson

Pausing for emphasis, Obama assured the audience he wasn't exaggerating the details.

'I'm not making this up,' Obama continued. 'He, the President of the United States, is spending time super-gluing gold medallions to the mantle in the Oval Office.' 

JD Vance's foul-mouthed meltdown over Elon Musk and tech billionaires

Obama, often called the Democratic Party's 'closer,' headlined the rally in Atlanta to boost key candidates ahead of the Nov. 3 election.

The former President's visit aims to rally support for Sen. Jon Ossoff, who is seeking reelection against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms, who is running against Republican Rick Jackson.

During a Saturday campaign appearance for Democrats in Ohio, Obama made a similar line of jokes at his successor's penchant for renovation projects, remarking that Trump 'should be on HGTV.' 

Taking a now infamous jab at the administration's decor, Obama said, 'He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,' a remark delivered despite pushback over the design of his own presidential library in South Side Chicago.

Hitting back on Monday before departing Joint Base Andrews for a campaign event in Mississippi, President Trump insisted his predecessor failed to properly maintain the executive residence, declaring, 'For you to say it's a Cheesecake Factory, that just shows why you were a lousy president.' 

Dismissing Obama's critique, Trump asserted that his predecessor simply does not understand because he is not a 'smart guy.'

'He's not smart at all because of the way he ran the country. Only a stupid person would run the country like that,' Trump said.

'We have to explain that to Obama because he doesn't understand it because he's not a smart guy,' continuing that Obama consistently overlooked 'dirt and filth' and walls that had not 'been cleaned for years.'

During a Saturday campaign appearance for Democrats in Ohio, Obama poked fun at his successor's passion for building projects, remarking that Trump 'should be on HGTV'

Hitting back at Barack Obama's weekend gibe comparing the refurbished White House to a chain restaurant, President Donald Trump insisted Monday that his predecessor failed to properly maintain the historic executive residence

'Guys like Obama don't see it... He doesn't see broken ornaments on a building,' Trump argued while defending his updates to the historic residence. 

Firmly standing by his work, the president concluded, 'I've taken care of the White House. I fixed it with the finest artisans in the world,' before adding, 'We have to explain to Obama that the White House is a symbol of America, and it has to be maintained properly.'

Which midterm races should YOU be watching? Enter your zip code in our exclusive election calculator

Obama's appearance highlights a flurry of political stops in Georgia.

Trump recently held campaign events in Dalton on Oct. 16 and Perry on Oct. 24.

Meanwhile, former Vice President Kamala Harris is scheduled to visit the state later this week, with plans to attend the Fulton County Democratic Party's annual gala on Friday.

A new Reuters/Ipsos poll finished on October 26 found that Trump's approval rating is at just 32 percent, with 66 percent of voters disapproving.

Democrats also led Republicans 53 to 44 percent among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot, after undecided voters' preferences were accounted for.

A majority of respondents claimed living costs were a big issue for them.

Donald TrumpObamaUS Midterm ElectionsGeorgia
news.summary: Former President Barack Obama took the stage in Georgia to campaign for Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, with a fresh attack against President Donald Trump.

news.title: Darline Graham Hit with Troubling Poll One Day Before Trump Rally
news.text: Darline Graham, Republican candidate for U.S. Senate in South Carolina, received a potentially troubling poll on Wednesday, just one day before President Donald Trump is scheduled to appear in the Palmetto State. The poll from The New York Times/Siena Research Institute shows that Graham and Democratic candidate Dr. Annie Andrews are tied at 48 percent and 3 percent don't know. The poll comes as Trump is set to rally with Graham on Thursday in Rock Hill, South Carolina. Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Trump won South Carolina during the 2024 presidential election versus then-Vice President Kamala Harris. The late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, Darline's brother, won the seat in the 2020 election cycle along with the primary in June. He died from aortic dissection due to arteriosclerotic cardiovascular disease, a preliminary examination by the D.C. Medical Examiner determined. He died in July at 71 years old, following what his office described as a "brief and sudden illness." Following his death, Darline was sworn into his seat just three days later, with the backing of Trump. Meanwhile, Trump's overall approval rating and ranking on specific policy issues like the economy, immigration, jobs and the ongoing war in Iran have recently slipped as households across America are consistently flagging affordability concerns. The polling lows come as Trump has crisscrossed the country in the lead-up to November 3 to rally for potentially vulnerable GOP candidates, including previous stops in South Carolina. Newsweek reached out to Graham and Andrews' campaigns via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know The poll shows that men prefer Graham 55 percent to Andrews' 40 percent, and the reverse for women, with 54 percent backing Andrews while 43 percent support Graham. Fifty-seven percent of Independents back Andrews versus 37 percent who support Graham. Graham landed majority support from white, 45-year-olds and up, white with and without a college degree, and Republican likely voters. The survey shows that 89 percent of 2024 Trump voters backed Graham compared to 8 percent of Trump voters who support Andrews. Graham's favorability in the poll is 44 percent compared to a 41 percent unfavorable rating. Andrews' favorability is 45 percent compared to a 29 percent unfavorable rating. The survey shows that 51 percent think Andrews would do a better job on the economy compared to 43 percent who say Graham would. On immigration, 50 percent said Graham would do a better job versus 44 percent who said Andrews would. Forty-nine percent said Andrews would do what is best for ordinary South Carolinians compared to 46 percent who said Graham would. The poll surveyed 707 likely voters in the state from October 19-26, 2026, with a 4.3 percent margin of error. The Cook Political Report rates the race as lean Republican and prediction market sites Kalshi and Polymarket both show Graham leading on Wednesday afternoon. D. Stephen Voss, political professor at the University of Kentucky, told Newsweek on Wednesday, "Polls have been trending toward the Democrats with increasing margins, so surprises would not be impossible if that trajectory continues after most polls have left the field. Even the best polls are only snapshots in time; they cannot predict the future. Still, most voters have made their decisions by late October, so Republicans can have a reasonable hope that their standing has bottomed out and that they'll still hold on in states like South Carolina that have been consistently tilted their way. "The big question mark hanging over all of these polls is whether Democrats will continue to exhibit the big enthusiasm gap in their favor that the party has enjoyed in lower-turnout special elections. Greater mobilization among Republican voters for these competitive statewide races would offer a cushion that the GOP until now has been lacking." Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, also told Newsweek on Wednesday, "It’s hard to believe, but that appears to be the poll at present. I think in the final couple days, a lot of Republicans are likely to 'come home,' out of sympathy if nothing else. But if Democrats can win there, then it’s hard to imagine that the Senate will remain out of their reach." What Other Polling Shows An InsiderAdvantage poll showed Graham with 46 percent compared to Andrews' 45 percent, Libertarian Kasie Whitener with 2 percent, Constitution Party nominee Mark Hackett with 3 percent and 4 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 1,200 likely voters in South Carolina from September 28-29, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.83 percent. A previous InsiderAdvantage survey last month also showed Graham with a slight lead with 45.1 percent compared to Andrews' 43.2 percent. The survey shows that 3.2 percent said another candidate while 8.5 percent were undecided. That poll surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 8-9, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.83 percent. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: The new poll shows Graham and Andrews tied in the race for U.S. Senate in South Carolina less than a week before midterms.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: Hasan Piker Puts Ted Cruz on Notice After $72M Lawsuit Against Jennings
news.text: Left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker took aim at Ted Cruz on Wednesday after the Republican senator shared allegations similar to the ones that led to conservative commentator Scott Jennings getting sued by the streamer for $72.5 million. “Hey ted you seen this?” Piker wrote on X, sharing a news report about his lawsuit against Jennings. Cruz had posted that Piker was “calling for Black people to be lynched,” sharing a clip and a link to footage that Piker alleges was edited to strip his remarks of their original context. It appears to be the same or very similar footage to the video of Piker that featured on the August 11 episode of The Scott Jennings Show. Newsweek has reached out to Jennings, Cruz and Piker for comment. The filing comes as prominent political figures on both sides of the aisle increasingly turn to the courts to challenge statements they say have damaged their reputations. Why Did Hasan Piker Sue Scott Jennings? Piker's complaint, filed in a federal court in Washington, D.C., Tuesday, alleges that Jennings combined footage from three different livestreams, rearranged Piker's comments, and removed the YouTube debate that the streamer had been responding to, in order to remove the context of his remarks and falsely suggest he was advocating racial violence. Jennings falsely told listeners that the streamer had a “plan of returning our country to lynchings,” while airing the edited video of Piker, according to the filing. Piker argued in his lawsuit that he had been reacting sarcastically to a Black conservative commentator in the debate who blamed “woke DAs” for policies harming Black Americans. The left-wing commentator is seeking $27.5 million in compensatory damages and $45 million in punitive damages from Jennings. “You have to remember, this is not just about Scott Jennings, although he certainly messed up,” Piker said about the lawsuit. “This is about truth in the media.” President Donald Trump has made litigation against media organizations a prominent feature of his political career, filing lawsuits over coverage and commentary he says have misrepresented him. Trump's legal strategy extended beyond news organizations to political adversaries. In 2022, Trump sued Hillary Clinton and others over what he alleged was a conspiracy to undermine his presidential campaign. A federal judge dismissed the case and later ordered Trump and his attorney to pay nearly $1 million in sanctions. Meanwhile, California Governor Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, has brought a separate multimillion-dollar defamation suit against Fox News. Cruz and Piker's Escalating Feud Cruz and Piker have clashed publicly in recent weeks. In September, Piker accused the Texas senator and other Republican officials of trying to prevent him from speaking at the University of Texas at Austin, framing their opposition to the event as a threat to his First Amendment rights. Cruz had called Piker an “America-hating Marxist” and accused him of celebrating political violence against Republicans. Cruz continued his criticism of Piker at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas on September 10, invoking the streamer's past comments about the September 11 attacks while attacking Democrats associated with him. “When Hasan Piker says America deserved 9/11, believe him,” Cruz said. He later questioned why Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed had not disavowed Piker. Cruz's remarks refer to comments Piker made during a livestream in August 2019, while responding to an interview in which Republican Representative Dan Crenshaw discussed the September 11 attacks and U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East. Piker said, “America deserved 9/11, dude,” prompting widespread criticism. Piker subsequently walked back the remark, calling it inappropriate and saying he had expressed himself poorly. He argued that U.S. military interventions and support for armed groups in the region had contributed to the conditions that led to the attacks, describing the relationship as a “boomerang effect.” Trump’s History of High-Profile Defamation Lawsuits Trump has repeatedly used lawsuits to challenge media organizations and, at times, political opponents over claims he says have damaged his reputation or undermined his political standing. Several cases have sought billions of dollars in damages, including disputes over television editing and reporting about his conduct. In December 2025, Trump sued the BBC for $10 billion over a documentary that edited excerpts of his January 6, 2021, speech. His complaint alleged that the editing misleadingly combined separate portions of the speech, creating the impression that he directly encouraged violence while omitting remarks about peaceful protest. The BBC apologized for the editing but denied that it defamed Trump and has said it will defend the case. The litigation remains ongoing, with a federal judge ordering Trump to sit for a deposition by December 11. Trump also sued ABC News and anchor George Stephanopoulos in March 2024 after the anchor repeatedly said on air that Trump had been found liable for rape in the civil case brought by E. Jean Carroll. A jury had found Trump liable for sexual abuse and defamation, rather than rape under the narrow definition applied by the jury. ABC settled the lawsuit in December 2024, agreeing to contribute $15 million toward Trump’s future presidential library and pay $1 million in legal fees. The network also published an editor’s note expressing regret. In another case, Trump sued CBS News over its editing of a 60 Minutes interview with then-Vice President Kamala Harris during the 2024 presidential campaign. Trump alleged that the editing deceptively presented Harris’ answers in a way that benefited her campaign. He initially sought $10 billion, later increasing the demand to $20 billion. CBS parent company Paramount Global agreed in July 2025 to pay $16 million to settle the case, with the money allocated to Trump’s future presidential library and legal fees. The settlement did not include an apology, and Paramount maintained that the lawsuit lacked merit. Gavin Newsom’s Lawsuit Against Fox News In June 2025, Newsom sued Fox News for $787 million, alleging that the network and host Jesse Watters misrepresented a phone conversation between Newsom and Trump and had falsely accused the California governor of lying about it. The dispute followed public disagreement over when the two politicians had spoken during a period of unrest in Los Angeles. Newsom alleged that Fox’s coverage distorted the timeline and damaged his reputation. Fox denied the allegations and sought to have the case dismissed. A Delaware judge rejected that effort in April 2026, allowing the lawsuit to proceed. The Delaware Supreme Court declined to consider an early appeal in August, and a trial was scheduled for March 2028. The case remains ongoing. Other Recent Defamation Cases Involving Democrats Other cases involving Democratic politicians illustrate how defamation disputes can emerge from political campaigns, social media and internal party conflicts. Virginia Democratic state Delegate Dan Helmer filed a $15 million defamation lawsuit in 2025 against fellow Democrats and a lawyer after allegations of sexual misconduct surfaced shortly before a congressional primary he ultimately lost. Helmer denied the allegations and claimed they were politically motivated. The case was settled with all parties by January 2026, but the terms were confidential. In Arkansas, former Democratic gubernatorial nominee Christopher Jones sued Republican state Sen. Bart Hester in May 2024 after Hester accused him on social media of taking a “Pro Hamas Terrorist position” in response to Jones’s comments about student protests over the war in Gaza. Jones argued that Hester had falsely conflated support for protesters with support for Hamas. Hester defended his comments as political speech. Jones voluntarily dismissed the lawsuit in May 2025. What Happens Next? While it's unclear if Piker will pursue legal action against Cruz, Piker’s lawsuit against Jennings is in its early stages. The streamer alleges that Jennings' portrayal of Piker harmed his reputation, caused emotional distress and threatened his professional interests. He is pursuing claims including defamation, defamation by implication and false light. Jennings will have an opportunity to respond and could seek to have the case dismissed. The parties could also reach a settlement before trial. If it proceeds, the legal battle is likely to focus on whether Jennings’ portrayal of Piker’s remarks constituted defamation. Under the standard established by the Supreme Court in New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, public officials must generally prove that a defamatory falsehood was published with “actual malice”—meaning knowledge that it was false or reckless disregard for whether it was false. The standard also applies to public figures under related Supreme Court decisions. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Hasan Piker took aim at Ted Cruz over his X post, warning him he'd sued a conservative commentator for similar comments.
news.author: Hannah Parry

news.title: Tim Walz's Praise of Peggy Flanagan Should Be a Giant Red Flag for Minnesota Voters
news.text:
There were a great many things that were problematic about Tim Walz. Going back to before he became Kamala Harris' running mate, he had interesting takes on socialism (calling it "neighborliness"), was exposed for lying about his service record, and really liked communist China. After joining Kamala's 2024 campaign, it became clear that he had more problems. Then we learned about the massive welfare fraud in Minnesota, including the "Feeding Our Future" scandal and fraud in Medicaid and childcare programs. 

It was so bad that Walz was forced to drop out of his reelection bid, and Sen. Amy Klobuchar is now running to be Minnesota's next governor.

Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan also has her sights set on higher office. She's running for the Senate, and voters should be aware that she was part of the administration that allowed the theft of billions of taxpayer dollars. In 2018, she skipped a hearing where a whistleblower said the fraud scandal would be "Minnesota's Watergate" and spent the next eight years pandering to the Somali community, a large source of the welfare fraud. She gave an "Outstanding Refugee" award to a fraudster, endorsed a state representative who reportedly tried to funnel money to fraudsters, and she's good friends with Nimco Ahmed, who is now facing investigations for fraud related to fake autism centers.

Flanagan's Republican opponent, Michelle Tafoya, has hammered Flanagan on the fraud issue.

There is a stark contrast in this race.My opponent has been the second in command of Minnesota for the last 8 years.What has happened under her watch? Billions in fraud. Decreased academic performance. Increased crime.In 6 days, we can give Peggy Flanagan a pink slip. pic.twitter.com/9KWrGEKVR5— Michele Tafoya (@Michele_Tafoya) October 28, 2026

Programs meant to help people in need should actually reach them.In Minnesota, fraudsters cashed in while the families who were counting on that support were left with nothing.Every stolen dollar meant a Minnesotan who needed help didn’t get it.First, Tim Walz and Peggy… pic.twitter.com/sVngYzlpjx— Michele Tafoya (@Michele_Tafoya) October 28, 2026

And it's important for Minnesota voters to remember that Tim Walz not only picked Flanagan to be his running mate, he spent years singing her praises.

In 2017, Walz chose Flanagan to be lieutenant governor, saying that "Peggy's vast knowledge and expertise will be something I rely on daily." He also said that Flanagan "has life experience that is different from mine but brought us to the same place, and always with joy and hopefulness."

He did this, according to the Star Tribune, to "both bolster his credibility with progressives and bring geographic balance as he mounts a bid from greater Minnesota." He also said that he and Flanagan have "a lot of shared values" that would help him "united this state."

In 2020, Walz said Flanagan helped him govern. "Every major decision she is there from the beginning and helps me see about them differently and think about them differently,” Walz said. “You have a 55-year-old rural white guy who was in the Army and coached football, and you have a 39-year-old indigenous woman who lived in St. Louis Park. That brings a wealth of [ways] to approach these issues." Walz also said Flanagan "taught him to be authentic."

"I thought I had to shape myself to being people who I thought were politicians, and I thought, I’ll never be able to give a speech like that. That’s not how I talk, that’s not how I think," he said. "It was [Flanagan] who said, 'You need to be your own self, and if that works as a candidate it works.'"

Of course, things may have soured between the two or Walz is putting distance there now to protect Flanagan's Senate run. Walz hasn't endorsed anyone in the Senate race, and his wife, Gwen Walz, endorsed Rep. Angie Craig in the primary. During a July debate between Flanagan and Craig, the moderator asked Flanagan about Walz's lack of endorsement.

"The governor is really clear very early on that he was going to stay neutral and I appreciate that," she said at the time. But for years, Walz was singing her praises, and Flanagan was a major part of the Walz administration.

Voters in Minnesota should remember this when they go to the polls.

news.title: Trump Voters May Help Abdul El-Sayed Defeat Mike Rogers in Michigan
news.text: Some Michigan voters who helped return President Donald Trump to the White House in 2024 plan to vote for Democrat Abdul El-Sayed for U.S. Senate, a crack in the president's coalition that could matter in a race most polls show is separated by a few points. Several of them live in Dearborn, a majority Arab American city that broke for Trump two years ago, largely out of anger over U.S. support for Israel's war in Gaza, and residents who backed him told The Washington Post this week that El-Sayed is now the one carrying the "America First" banner. El-Sayed, a physician and former Wayne County public health director, is running against Republican former Representative Mike Rogers for the seat Democratic Senator Gary Peters is giving up. He will be the first Muslim in the U.S. Senate if he wins. Michigan hasn't sent a Republican to the Senate since 1994. Rogers nearly ended that streak in 2024, losing to Democrat Elissa Slotkin by less than a percentage point on the same night Trump carried the state. Newsweek reached out to the El-Sayed and Rogers campaigns for comment via email. Mike Rogers vs. Abdul El-Sayed: Latest Polls El-Sayed has led every major public poll released in the last two weeks, mostly by margins inside the error range. His best number came from Glengariff Group, which surveyed 600 likely voters for The Detroit News and WDIV-TV from October 19-22 and found him ahead 51 percent to 45 percent. Four percent were undecided. Independents moved, too. For the first time this cycle, Glengariff had El-Sayed winning them, 45.5 percent to 40 percent. "The margin you're leading by among independents tends to be the margin that you win by," pollster Richard Czuba told The Detroit News. The survey even put El-Sayed slightly ahead in the Upper Peninsula and northern Michigan, Trump country for years. Other polls are closer. Marist University had the race at 50 percent for El-Sayed to Rogers' 48 percent among 1,185 likely voters polled October 15-18. InsiderAdvantage, surveying 1,200 likely voters October 21-22, found El-Sayed up by a point, 47 percent to 46 percent, with four minor-party candidates at 1 percent apiece. A Michigan State University Institute for Public Policy and Social Research survey conducted with YouGov over a longer window, October 2-19, showed El-Sayed up 48 percent to 46 percent among 836 likely voters. Why Some Michigan Voters Who Chose Trump in 2024 Are Backing Abdul El-Sayed Trump took about 42 percent of the vote in Dearborn in 2024, beating then-Vice President Kamala Harris in a city Democrats had treated as safe. Green Party nominee Jill Stein pulled roughly 18 percent there, much of it a protest vote over Gaza. Among Arab Americans nationally, the mood has since shifted. In a Washington Post-Schar School poll, 58 percent said they support Democrats for Congress, after the group split evenly between Trump and Harris. Two-thirds of Arab Americans who voted for Trump still approve of the job he's doing overall. On Israel's war in Gaza, 54 percent disapprove. The Post interviewed three Dearborn residents who voted for Trump in 2024 and now back El-Sayed. They said the president failed to end wars in Lebanon and Yemen and bring down prices. Mustapha El-Jaroudi, a two-time Trump voter, said Rogers would “put Israel first.” None regret their Trump vote, but all three said El-Sayed now best reflects “America First.” Campaign finance records reviewed by Newsweek show where Dearborn’s loyalties sit. Donors in Dearborn and Dearborn Heights gave El-Sayed about $131,000 in itemized contributions from mid-July through September, from 212 people, according to Federal Election Commission filings. Rogers listed 11 donors from the same two cities who gave him about $9,100. The money kept coming after the primary. Dearborn-area donors gave El-Sayed roughly $45,700 in July, ahead of his August 4 primary win, and about $45,000 in September, after the general election campaign was underway. Among them were physicians, pharmacists, attorneys and small business owners, and a Dearborn Heights city councilman. El-Sayed has gone looking for these voters. One of his ads ran only on Fox News and Newsmax and stitched together clips of conservative hosts—Tucker Carlson and Jesse Watters among them—saying kind things about him. On the campaign trail, he blames Trump's war with Iran for what Michiganders pay at the pump, where a gallon of unleaded gasoline averaged $4.59 this month against $2.88 a year ago, according to AAA Michigan figures cited by The Detroit News. Latest Developments in the Michigan Senate Race Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. pushed the fight over El-Sayed's faith further on Monday. Campaigning in Grand Rapids for Rogers and Republican gubernatorial nominee John James, Kennedy told the crowd that "talking about the Muslim Brotherhood is not Islamophobia," then turned to Arabs as a whole. "There's 500 million Arabs in the world. And yet they don't produce science," Kennedy said. "They don't win the Nobel Prize. They don't win the Fields Prize." Egyptian chemist Ahmed Zewail won the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1999, Egyptian novelist Naguib Mahfouz won the literature prize in 1988 and Yemeni activist Tawakkol Karman shared the 2011 Peace Prize. Michigan has the highest share of residents reporting Arab ancestry of any state, about 2.2 percent, according to Census Bureau data. Kennedy spoke about a race in which El-Sayed's religion has become a central line of attack. Rogers has repeatedly tied him, without evidence, to the Muslim Brotherhood, and pressed it again at their final debate on October 21: "Are you for America, or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?" Trump himself has mocked El-Sayed's middle name, Mohamed, and told reporters on his way to a Port Huron rally on October 25: "We don't want to see a jihadist senator." El-Sayed, who has disavowed the group, called Rogers' question "shameful." Democrats and Muslim advocates describe the attacks as Islamophobic, an effort to cast the man who would be the first Muslim senator as less than fully American. Former President Barack Obama made that case at a Detroit rally on October 24, comparing it to the birther conspiracy once aimed at him. "This stuff didn't work on me," Obama said. "Not in Michigan. It's not going to work on Abdul." El-Sayed has hit back. He calls Rogers a Trump "sock puppet," told debate viewers to play "MAGA bingo" with his answers and has made the pro-Israel lobby a recurring target. "That's what you get when you have an AIPAC-backed politician," he said during the debate. AIPAC's super PAC, the United Democracy Project, is sending up to $9 million to a pro-Rogers super PAC after the pre-election disclosure deadline, The New York Times reported. Asked about the group's help, Rogers said: "I'll take all of that help." El-Sayed has also drawn criticism for his own words. After an attack on a Detroit-area synagogue this year by a man who had lost relatives in an Israeli strike on Lebanon, El-Sayed said that "hurt people hurt people." He later apologized, saying: "To anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I'm really sorry." El-Sayed practically dared Trump to come to Michigan, betting that the visit would remind voters whose candidate Rogers is. Port Huron is in a part of the state Trump carried with more than 66 percent of the vote in 2024. Rogers has edged away from the president on at least one issue, the tariffs on Canada, which he said hurt Michigan's auto industry. The money keeps coming. Federal Election Commission filings show that El-Sayed raised about $30.7 million from mid-July through September, more than three times Rogers' $9.7 million. Republicans hold the edge on television, $105 million to $76 million in ad spending, according to AdImpact data reported by Axios, and Bridge Michigan counts more than $205 million in total disclosed spending on the race. Jewish Opposition to Abdul El-Sayed May Not Matter in Michigan Race The Muslim voter advocacy group Emgage estimates that there are more than 200,000 registered Muslim voters in Michigan. By comparison, Michigan is home to roughly 105,000 Jewish adults, about 1.4 percent of the state's electorate, according to the American Jewish Population Project at Brandeis University. Republican-aligned estimates run higher, up to 130,000. "It is important to remember that no state has a higher percentage of Arab-American residents in the U.S. than Michigan. The Jewish population is less than half that of the Arab-American population there," Jim Kessler, executive vice president for policy at the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way, told Newsweek. Arab American and Muslim are overlapping but distinct groups. Many of Michigan's Arab American residents are Chaldean and other Christians, while the state's Muslim community also includes South Asian and Black Muslims. Turnout narrows the gap, Kessler warned. Jewish voters participate at high rates, while Muslim turnout has historically lagged. In the 2018 midterms, 50 percent of registered Muslim voters in Michigan cast ballots, according to Emgage. In 2024, a Council on American-Islamic Relations exit poll of Michigan Muslim voters found that Stein received 59 percent support, Trump 22 percent and Harris 14 percent. Trump won more than 42 percent of the vote in Dearborn, where more than 55 percent of residents are of Middle Eastern descent, up from 30 percent four years earlier. Many others sat out. Early voting turnout was 25 percent in Dearborn and 24 percent in Hamtramck, against 44 percent statewide. Those voters already delivered for El-Sayed once. In the August primary, he received 16,265 more votes than Michigan Representative Haley Stevens across Dearborn and Dearborn Heights alone, more than his statewide margin over her of a little more than 14,000 votes, in unofficial results. Why Is the Michigan Senate Race Important in the 2026 Midterms? Democrats need a net gain of four seats to flip the Senate, where Republicans hold 53. The Cook Political Report rates Michigan a toss-up, the only Democratic-held seat with that rating, which makes it the likeliest place for Republicans to make up ground lost elsewhere. Election Day is November 3. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jenna deJong and Dave Siminoff.

news.title: How anti-Arab rhetoric became a political weapon in America’s midterm elections
news.text:
LONDON: For the Arab Americans of Michigan, whose backing was credited with having helped to return Donald Trump to the presidency, there was perhaps more than a little irony in the president’s health secretary choosing the state as the platform for his anti-Arab comments on Monday.

Speaking at a campaign event in Grand Rapids, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. claimed that Arabs “don’t produce ​science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win ⁠the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature.”

His comments were demonstratively false. Arabs have won all of those prizes and have produced a breadth and volume of literature to rival that of any culture.

In 1988, Egyptian author Naguib Mahfouz was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature for a body of work that amounted to “an Arabian narrative art that applies to all mankind.”

In 2025, Palestinian American Omar Yaghi was one of three scientists awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing “a new form of molecular architecture … to harvest water from desert air, capture carbon dioxide, store toxic gases or catalyze chemical reactions.”

But Kennedy, who is often accused of taking an unscientific approach to his public health brief, did not seem overly concerned about facts, but rather with denigrating Egyptian American Abdul El-Sayed, the Democrat nominee in the race to become a Michigan senator.

It was, as El-Sayed’s spokesman Cole Wozniak told The New York Times, “rich to have an anti-scientist come to Michigan to lecture a doctor with two doctoral degrees who has spent his entire career working on public health.”

With the Nov. 3 midterms imminent, and voter support for President Trump at an all-time low, the Republican party is facing the very real possibility of the Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress — and the Michigan race could dictate which party controls the Senate.

Michigan, as Dr. James Zogby, the president of the Arab American Institute wrote on Monday, “is this year’s most important election.”

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim in the Senate, “a breakthrough that hasn’t been lost on Republicans and President Trump, who have made a determined effort to exploit it at every turn.”

Born and raised in Michigan, El-Sayed’s campaign has focused on America’s cost of living crisis. He describes himself as a “public servant running for US Senate because it shouldn’t be this hard to get by.”

The Republicans have run TV ads alleging that El-Sayed’s mother was affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood in the 1970s, even though, said Zogby, “El-Sayed’s parents separated when he was three; she moved back to Egypt and he grew up with his father in Michigan.”

Planted hecklers have raised the issue repeatedly at El-Sayed’s campaign events, although the candidate has only gained admiration — and a social media following — for the way he has handled them.

In Grand Rapids on Monday, Kennedy was campaigning on behalf of Mike Rogers, the Republican party candidate for Michigan, who is facing a serious challenge from El-Sayed.

His comments about Arabs and Muslims echoed those of the president. Trump has repeatedly mocked El-Sayed, whom he always refers to as “Mohammed” (“Why? Because I feel like it”).

At a rally in Detroit on Saturday, El-Sayed responded: “My name and my faith are not the reason you can’t afford your gas (and) not the reason you can’t afford your groceries.”

Both Rogers and Trump are accused of leveraging Islamophobia in an attempt to sway the election.

In a televised debate on Oct. 8, the Republican nominee questioned whether a member of El-Sayed’s family might be on a “watchlist.” The following day, Trump posted on social media: “Mohammad is a Jihadist lunatic who hates our Country.”

On Sunday, in remarks at a rally in Port Huron, Trump again labeled El-Sayed a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists.” He then suggested that, if elected, he would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

He also raised the specter of the 9/11 attacks, seemingly equating the need to block El-Sayed from office with the courage of the passengers who fought back on Flight 93.

Sadly, Zogby told Arab News, “we’ve seen periods like this before. In the 1980s, the political cartoons would be Arabs holding money bags, supporting this candidate, (and) I remember candidates giving money back: ‘They don’t want any Arab money.’

“If somebody had an Arab American on their campaign staff, AIPAC (the powerful American Israel Public Affairs Committee lobbying group) would come and say: ‘You’ve got to fire him, or else we won’t support your candidacy.’

“People lost their jobs. It was a very difficult environment.”

What’s different now, he said, “is that the bullhorn of the president is uniquely powerful. We’ve not seen it before.

“I remember one of George W. Bush’s campaign ads had a kind of ominous anti-Arab, anti-Muslim tone to it, but we protested, and they pulled it.

“But we’ve never had a situation where the President of the United States says it over and over again, and does so every day and every night, and in such vicious ways.”

Other Republicans have been following the president’s lead. Earlier this month, Republican senator John Kennedy, campaigning in Detroit for Rogers, even suggested that El-Sayed probably slept “in a bin Laden shirt.”

When Zohran Mamdani was elected as the first ever Muslim mayor of New York City in November 2025, Republican congresswoman Nancy Mace commented: “After 9/11 we said ‘Never Forget.’ I think we sadly have forgotten.”

In March, an Alabama senator reposted a photograph of Mamdani taking part in an Iftar dinner, alongside a picture of one of the 9/11 attacks. “The enemy,” wrote Sen. Tommy Tuberville, “is inside the gates.”

That, however, was mild compared with a social media post that month from Tennessee Rep. Andy Ogles, who wrote that “Muslims don’t belong in American society. Pluralism is a lie.”

He responded to criticism by adding “paperwork doesn’t magically make you American ... Muslims are unable to assimilate; they all have to go back.”

In the run-up to the 2024 presidential election, Trump actively wooed the Arab American community.

Dismayed by the Biden administration’s support for Israel amid the Gaza war, many Arab Americans rejected Kamala Harris in favor of Trump, who had promised to bring peace to the Middle East.

In the Detroit suburb of Dearborn, where 60 percent of the population are Arab American, Biden received 30,000 votes in 2020. In 2024 Harris lost half of those votes, while Trump’s share jumped from 13,000 in 2020 to 18,000.

But since Trump’s return to office, Arab Americans could be forgiven for thinking they may have backed the wrong horse.

In 2024, Trump’s outreach to the community was facilitated by an organization called Arab Americans for Trump, founded that year by Palestinian American businessman Bishara Bahbah.

In 2025, in protest at Trump’s proposed takeover of Gaza, the group changed its name to Arab Americans for Peace. Trump’s latest attacks on El-Sayed have done nothing to heal the rift.

On Saturday, Bahbah told CNN that Trump’s “racist remarks are turning off the Arab and Muslim communities, and I’m sure turning off black Americans and Latinos as well.

“Mocking people because of who they are is just downright stupid and racist.”

There may, however, be something else motivating the verbal assault. Zogby highlighted that El-Sayed has been “a clear and consistent critic of US support for the Israeli genocide in Gaza.”

This, he wrote, explained why so much pro-Israel “dark money” has been funneled into defeating him via “super PACs” — Political Action Committees that can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money to influence elections — and “independent expenditure funds that are not required to report donors before elections.”

However Kennedy’s remarks might have played among Trump’s voter base, they have shocked many American academics.

On Monday, Dr. Peter Hotez, dean of the National School of Tropical Medicine at Baylor and Texas Children’s Hospital, posted on X that his former colleague Ahmed Zewail, the Egyptian American scientist and 1999 Nobel laureate in chemistry, “would disagree” with Kennedy.

“God rest his soul he didn’t have to endure this,” he said. “And of course RFK Jr forgets that it was the Arab scientists of the Middle Ages who kept Aristotle, Hippocrates, Galen alive to hand it down in the Renaissance.”

For Arab Americans considering how to vote in the midterms, Kennedy’s remarks stand in sharp contrast to comments that were made by President Joe Biden in March 2023, on the occasion of National Arab American Heritage Month.

In a presidential proclamation, Biden celebrated “the immeasurable contributions of Arab Americans to our Nation.”

Their achievements, he added, “are reflected in the arts and sciences; in businesses and faith communities; in classrooms and hospitals; and in police stations, firehouses, and every branch of the military.”

Arab Americans were also “proudly serving throughout my Administration, bringing a diversity of expertise that helps make this country stronger, more prosperous, and more just.”

Until recently, the text of Biden’s Proclamation 10539 could be viewed on the White House website. Today, the link is dead.

news.title: You Won't Believe What Kamala Harris Just Said About Impeaching Trump
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris cautioned Democrats against impeaching President Donald Trump if they regain control of the House in the midterm elections.

During an appearance on The Parnas Perspective podcast, the host asked, “Let's say Democrats win the House and the Senate next week. What would your recommendation be to leadership in Congress? Would it be to go the investigations route and potentially an impeachment one day, or would it be go pass policy and force the president to veto it?”

“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea,” Harris replied. “Okay, just to be honest with you, I just— because we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that's where the time should be spent.”

The former vice president recalled the prior two impeachment efforts, which ultimately failed, and said Democrats “have to just also agree that our attitude has to be to get stuff done, and the tone and our kind of orientation around it has to be kind of ruthless.”

Harris further stated that she believes “there are a lot of leaders in Congress right now on the Democratic side who are thankfully putting a lot of thought into day one when we take back the gavel.”

Let's not sit around clinking glasses of champagne, because as far as I'm concerned, the election, the night of the election, the day after, when, God willing, we win, that's not the end of this phase. That's the beginning of what we got to get done in terms of action, not just words.

Kamala Harris: I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea. We have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that’s where the time should be spent. I was in the Senate for the last go-round, and the votes aren’t there. I think after the election, we all have to just also agree that our attitude has to be to get stuff done…— Acyn (@Acyn) October 27, 2026

While some Democrats have avoided using the “I” word, some have already tried impeaching Trump during his second term.

However, others appear to agree with Harris — at least for now. "Literally no Democrats are talking about this," Rep. Pete Aguilar (CA-33) told Punchbowl News. "This is not something that comes up in our discussions at all."

Rep. Henry Cuellar (TX-28) said, “We’ve seen this twice already” and that “To do it a third time won’t work.”

President Trump has said on multiple occasions that if Democrats win back the House, they will impeach him again.

He’s right. That’s exactly what they will do.

Democrats have to play it cool since the midterms are close. They can’t run on “we’re totally gonna impeach the Orange Man What Is Bad™ if y’all vote for us.” They have to convince the public that they will take action on their economic problems.

But this doesn’t mean they won’t immediately file articles of impeachment five minutes after taking office in January. If they win, the nation will be subjected to Impeach Trump Part Three, which will likely go over about as well as the third Godfather sequel.

news.title: Arellano: The Dolores Huerta I'll remember
news.text: The rambunctious teenagers crammed into a lecture hall suddenly went quiet when a woman old enough to be their great-grandmother, and smaller in stature than many of them, approached the podium. Dolores Huerta was about to speak. At the summer conference for Latino high school students at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, in the early 2010s, I was the keynote speaker, with a hell of an opener before me. Huerta didn't talk for long, but I don’t think I’ve ever seen an audience as mesmerized. She said little about her distinguished life. Nothing about her many awards, her decades fighting to improve conditions for farmworkers across the U.S., her unlikely trajectory from the daughter of a coal miner to one of this country’s premier labor leaders and a Latina civil rights titan with few peers. No, Huerta focused on the young people before her. She challenged them to better themselves — that’s how communities improve, she argued. She made them laugh, she made them cheer, she brought tears to the eyes of some and concluded with the rebel chant long associated with her that we shouted in unison: Sí se puede. It can happen. The students gathered around her afterward for a group photo, and then she left as unceremoniously as she had arrived. Afterward, I asked the organizers why they didn’t have Dolores — everyone in my world called her by her first name, even if we didn’t know her personally, because that's how much she was a part of our lives — speak for a full hour, as I did. They said she had other things to do but wouldn't miss a chance to talk to students, charging a pittance compared with her usual speaking fee, and nowhere near the $25,000 a prominent Latina author had demanded. That is the Huerta so many are mourning after the news that she died of cancer Wednesday at age 96. Her legacy is secured in American history, but her daily calendar shows why she mattered so much to so many. Latinos long respected Huerta's career but didn't truly embrace her until her señora era, when she became our collective matriarch, in addition to the mother of 14 children. At a moment in Huerta's life when she could have faded into retirement and no one would have faulted her, she seemingly was everywhere all the time, because her work was nowhere near done. Because it never is. I ran into her multiple times in the 15 years after we first met — at protests and rallies where she was a speaker, at talks she gave to college students and community groups. She'd appear unannounced at art galleries and movie screenings just to show support for up-and-coming artists and filmmakers. One time during the COVID years, cartoonist Lalo Alcaraz, acting legend Cheech Marín and I were holding a tequila-fueled Zoom fundraiser for Marín's Chicano art museum when Huerta popped on our screens to gently tell us to stop making pendejos of ourselves. People couldn't believe how approachable she was, how she never seemed to say no to an autograph, a photo request, a chance to hear the stories of others and to truly care about each and every admirer. But giving so much of yourself inevitably comes with a cost. We all found out what Huerta personally lost when she revealed to the New York Times this year that her United Farm Workers co-founder Cesar Chavez had raped her and fathered two of her children during the 1960s. Huerta told the newspaper that she stayed quiet about the abuse for decades because she didn’t want to torpedo el movimiento that they had created. Latinos everywhere collectively mourned what she had endured and marveled that it didn't stop her activism, which continued until very recently. I wish I could have spoken to Dolores about the sacrifices she made in the name of all of us. But our relationship — never a personal one, but close enough that we greeted each other whenever we inevitably crossed paths — soured in later years. The last time we talked, she harangued me for having openly criticized Chavez’s opposition to illegal immigrants. “You have it all wrong on Cesar,” Huerta said over the phone while on a train heading to a conference, maintaining her stance even after I reminded her that UFW recordings showed her pushing back against the derogatory slurs against immigrants that he freely used. She invited me to meet her in Bakersfield, where her nonprofit is located, to talk more about it, an offer I sadly never took up. It was a reminder that Huerta was human and never perfect, like too many lionized leaders. She excused Chavez’s personal vendettas against critics for way too long and dismissed progressive Latino activists who criticized her for cozying up to establishment Democrats like Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris. But that won't be the Dolores I’ll remember. The Dolores who always will be in my mind is from that high school conference so long ago. I'll always remember her smile as wide as the brim of her hat, happy that young people wanted to do better, proud that she was able to help them — and ready to do more, because we all can. Sí se puede.
news.summary: People couldn't believe how approachable she was, how she never seemed to say no to an autograph, a photo request, a chance to hear the stories of others.

news.title: DOJ to send election monitors to Northwest Indiana
news.text:
Ella Kelly usually votes early, but she’s especially happy she got it done Tuesday.

The grandmother from Gary, Indiana, visited the Lake County Government Complex in Crown Point to cast her ballot a week before the Nov. 3 midterm election.

“It’s much more convenient,” Kelly said. “That’s why I’ve been voting like this for the past five years.”

The Department of Justice informed state officials it plans to send election monitors to polling places in two majority-Democratic counties. Besides Lake County, in Northwest Indiana, it will also will send the monitors to Marion County, home to the capital, Indianapolis.

In a statement, the department announced that nationwide, it will have about 1,000 monitors in place to monitor for potential violations to federal law, which will be reviewed after election day. It called the monitoring “routine,” but the announcement concerns some Democratic officials as well as some residents, including Kelly.

“I think it’s a scare tactic; it’s a form of intimidation,” Kelly said. “It’s a way of controlling people and causing trouble.”

Lake and Marion counties are historically blue areas in a mostly-red state, and in 2024 both were carried by Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris — in Marion County, Harris’ margin was nearly 28 percentage points.

Tuesday’s midterm includes the race for the 1st Congressional District seat now held by Frank J. Mrvan, a Democrat. His opponent is Republican Barb Regnitz, a Porter County commissioner.

Regnitz has Trump’s endorsement in a district stretching from Gary to Michigan City, spanning three counties.

Last year, President Donald Trump pushed but failed to get Indiana Republicans to redraw the state’s congressional map to make the 1st and 7th Congressional Districts to favor Republicans. The 7th Congressional District includes Indianapolis. The seat is now held by Democratic incumbent Andre Carson.

The move by Trump’s DOJ isn’t sitting well with Lake County Democrats.

“My position is one of concern in that there’s not been any sort of complaint they’re following up on,” said Michael Repay, chairman of the Lake County Democratic Central Committee and a county commissioner. “Another concern is that this Department of Justice doesn’t seem to have a good track record for ensuring civil rights.”

Lake County GOP Chair Randy Niemeyer said he supports the DOJ’s move.

“We welcome oversight; we don’t have anything to hide,” Niemeyer, who is also a county councilman, said. “[Federal monitors] were here in 2016 under the Obama administration and I don’t recall there being any issues of voter intimidation. It’s not like they’re going to be stormtroopers.”

Niemeyer said the monitors won’t have access to polling places since they do not possess the proper credentials. He sees the monitoring as fairly routine.

“It’s two counties where you see the highest number of votes in the state, the two largest counties and most precincts,” Niemeyer said. “I think that probably has more to do with it than anything,”

Michelle Fajman, director of the Lake County Board of Elections and Registration, said her office was set to meet with federal and state officials this week to go over what is expected.

Fajman said about a dozen election monitors will visit polling sites in the county, but the specific sites remain unclear. The monitors may ask voters exit questions but only outside the polls and participation is not required, he explained.

“Intimidation is always a concern; I cannot determine how someone is going to feel about that,” Fajman said. “But voters don’t have to stop and talk to anyone. If they don’t want to answer their exit polls, they don’t have to.”

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita, a Republican and unwavering Trump ally, supports the move by the DOJ.

“I want every election to be secure and run as effectively as possible, so that we can feel confident that our votes count and that the results are accurate, fair, and legitimate,” Rokita said. “To help make that happen, I welcome the Department of Justice sending election monitors into Indiana on Nov. 3, and maybe even before.”

Michael Puente is a reporter and weekend anchor for WBEZ. Reach him at mpuente@wbez.org.
news.author: Michael Puente

news.title: Reporter Allowed To Cover Peter Thiel’s Antichrist Lecture Just So Happened To Work For Outlet He Funded
news.text:
Out of everyone who attended billionaire-entrepreneur Peter Thiel’s lecture series on the Antichrist, only a reporter from the Thiel-funded Pirate Wires was allowed to disclose what was said at the event. 

Attendees came to the Grand Lodge of Tennessee Free and Accepted Masons in Nashville for four consecutive Mondays starting Sept. 28 to hear Thiel’s lecture series on the Antichrist. Only Thiel-funded Pirate Wires’ G. B. Rango was permitted to share his experience at the off-the-record lecture series. 

“[The article] is my best attempt at a faithful reconstruction of the events and arguments from my memory, notes, and occasional reference to online posts from other attendees,” Rango said in his article, “Inside Peter Thiel’s Nashville Antichrist Lectures.” 

Funded by Thiel, Pirate Wires was created in 2020 by Michael Solana, former vice president at Thiel’s venture capital firm, Founder’s Fund. Neither Pirate Wires, Thiel nor Rango responded to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment. 

The Daily Caller’s request to cover the event was denied.

TIM DILLON: That’s why Peter Thiel’s lecturing about Satan and saying Satan’s going to be somebody right here on Earth who’s going to try to limit AI. The person who says, hey, we should put some safeguards on AI, that’s all Peter Thiel requires for you to be considered Satan. Seems like a very loose definition of the Antichrist.— Grace Chong, MBI (@gc22gc) September 6, 2026

“The Antichrist, says Thiel, will mark the totalitarian termination of philosophy,” Rango wrote.

In traditional Christian eschatology, the Antichrist is the false prophet who will deny Christ and reign before the Second Coming, according to theologian Christopher Rowland. 

“Peter Thiel has long referred to ‘peace and safety,’ sourced from 1 Thessalonians 5:3, as the ‘slogan’ of the Antichrist,” Rango wrote. Thiel thinks that the Antichrist will assume authoritarian power through the promise of peace, Rango claimed. 

The lectures at the Free Mason lodge ventured off into other topics, like transhumanism, according to Rango.

“[Thiel] noted that Matthew 10:8 is an imperative (‘Heal the sick, cleanse the lepers, raise the dead, cast out devils’) and posited that, perhaps, transhumanism does not go far enough, and that Christian transformation goes even further than that,” Rango said.

On the subject of artificial intelligence (AI), Thiel suggested that it won’t be AI itself, but rather the “AI Safetyists” espousing “apocalyptic doomerism” who will provide the groundwork for the rise of the Antichrist, Rango claimed. 

Thiel made a point of calling out Pope Leo XIV, calling him a “useful idiot” for writing Magnifica Humanitas, an encyclical on AI, which Thiel dubs as granting “cultural authority to AI doomers,” Rango wrote. (RELATED: Smoking, Immortality And Silicon Valley’s Machine God)

Because of the United States’ political and cultural authority, Thiel mused on the possibility of presidential hopefuls being the Antichrist. Thiel ruled out New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as the Antichrist because he cannot become president. He considered former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom as more likely candidates. 

“Look for a person who would be a very bad president of the United States,” Rango claims Thiel said on identifying the Antichrist. 

Thiel does not believe President Donald Trump is the Antichrist because he is not popular enough, Rango remarked. 

Xi Jinping, president of China, might be the “second-coming of Hitler,” but not the Antichrist, Thiel said, according to Rango. 

Thiel’s Nashville lecture series at the Freemasons’ lodge is the latest in his attempts to stir intellectual curiosity in the Antichrist. In previous lectures in Rome and San Francisco, Thiel suggested AI skeptics and climate alarmists are “legionnaires of the Antichrist,” and implicated Greta Thunberg as a potential candidate for the end-times ruler.
news.summary: ‘Second-coming of Hitler’
news.author: Michael Solana,Pete Peterson

news.title: Kamala Harris Urges Democrats to Back Off Donald Trump Impeachment Push: 'It's Not a Good Idea'
news.text:
Vice President Kamala Harris has warned Democrats to be wary of potentially impeaching President Donald Trump, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

The former presidential candidate fears that the Democrats, while they could get the numbers if they win the midterms, don't have the energy to do it correctly.Kamala Harris Warns Democrats Against Trump ImpeachmentWhile speaking with Aaron Parnas of MeidasTouch, Harris was asked what advice she would give to incoming Democrats who manage to win a seat in Congress. 

"I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you," she said. "Just because we have limited resources, and I think the energy and the resources need to be put into accountability, need to be put into investigations. And that’s where the time should be spent."

The 62-year-old argued an impeachment was a losing battle in the end, despite Democrats advertising it as an option during their campaigning. While the House of Representatives might gain the power to impeach Trump, the Senate won't flip to the Democrats.Trump's Prior Impeachments Failed to Result in ConvictionHarris reflected on previous attempts made to impeach Trump.

In his first term, while the Democrats controlled the House of Representatives, Trump blocked Congress' authority to aid Ukraine in 2019. Additionally, he attempted to overturn the 2020 election, which resulted in the January 2026 Capitol Insurrection.

For each case, he was impeached. However, the Senate was unable to convict him or remove him from office, as it needed a two-thirds majority vote to do so.

Harris is intimately familiar with the Senate's failure to convict, as she was representing the state of California in the chamber. "The votes aren't there," she said.Kamala Harris Pushes Democrats to Be 'Ruthless'Instead, Harris wants Democrats to focus on unity within the party to "get stuff done." She argued their approach can't be cavalier, but rather "ruthless." She wants to combat the very "ruthless" behavior of the Republican Party, calling them "cruel."

However, Harris wants her Party to ditch cruelty in favor of a more "uncompromising" approach.

She said, "Like, not sit around, you know, being genteel about the relationships and instead actually get stuff done, whether it be about accountability or restoring, for example, what they took in terms of the Medicaid cuts, restoring what we need to do around some check-and-balance around this war nobody wants. And there's no time to wait."Dems Favored in Midterm ElectionsThe midterm elections will occur on November 3, 2026, with some states offering early voting. Early polling suggests Americans can expect a blue wave, with Democrats projected to win key seats in Congress.

As of October 27, nearly 33 million Americans cast their vote early. The midterm elections are expected to have an unprecedented turnout for a non-presidential election. The early voters have already made up about a quarter of votes previously cast in the 2022 midterms.

Registered Democrats have voted at higher rates than Republicans in the 27 states that track the data. However, Republicans are reportedly less likely to cast their vote early than Democrats.

Democrats are currently leading in many polls.
news.summary: Former Vice President Kamala Harris asked Democrats to reconsider impeaching President Donald Trump if they take control of Congress.
news.author: Alex West

news.text:

BAIER: No, no.

BAIER: I'm not.

BAIER: This is a specific -- his campaign said today --

BAIER: Thank you.

EL-SAYED: In a 2012 statement in a letter --

BAIER: You don't want to walk that back?

EL-SAYED: You're going to pull that out of context.

BAIER: I'm not pulling it out.

EL-SAYED: You're going to ask questions about my allegiance. Let me just be brief.

BAIER: This is Rogers's campaign -- I'm just asking you about that.

EL-SAYED: Don't be Rogers's campaign.

EL-SAYED: Be a journalist.

EL-SAYED: So, as a journalist, if you're asking the question about my allegiance to the Constitution, I have never been a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. I never will be a member of the Muslim Brotherhood. I am interested in serving the United States. I'm interested in swearing an oath to the Constitution that every Senator has swore an oath to. If the question about my faith is the issue which Mike Rogers wants it to be, I think it is sad and beneath him and frankly, beneath the President of the United States to make that an issue because, under our Constitution, you're guaranteed the right to pray as you choose to pray.

MIKE ROGERS, MICHIGAN REPUBLICAN SENATE NOMINEE: He's accepted campaign donations from organizations, as I said, and even the literal spokesman from the Muslim Brotherhood. I'll tell you, as a former FBI agent, I can tell you we would call that a clue. (pause for audience reaction) But we sure know that Abdul el-Sayed does not belong anywhere near the United States Senate.

MIKA BRZEZINSKI: Oh my God. Republican nominee for U.S. Senate in Michigan, Mike Rogers, once again alleging his Democratic opponent, Abdul el-Sayed, has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, a connection el-Sayed continues to disavow. As we saw in that Fox News interview from Friday with Bret Baier.

SCARBOROUGH: Well, you know, the thing is, I mean, again, I will tell you for people who don't know Mike Rogers, I served with him.

BRZEZINSKI: That's not Mike Rogers.

SCARBOROUGH: And Mike was -- I liked him very much. He was a solid Michigan guy. I say that because I -- I have relatives in Michigan, and I love -- love solid Michigan people unless they cheer for the Wolverines and -- but he -- he was a serious guy. He -- he had great impeccable national security credentials. And it's just sad. It really is. And I do mean this. It is sad to see him shrink to this level, to stoop to this level, talking about how because he's a Muslim, that he's some terrorist because his mother worked with some charities, that he's like a member of the Muslim Brotherhood, or he's this with the Muslim Brotherhood. I got to say, good for him also, when Bret (Baier) was coming after him again, just trying to parrot all of the hate -- hate attacks from the Rogers campaign, saying, "Don't -- don't -- don't be a Rogers campaign person, be a journalist."

And, of course, there is a back story there. You know what he did with Kamala Harris and misleading her? Playing -- playing, I think -- I think video was wrong there. Yeah, so it is -- it's unfortunate. And I just do want to go back. I just have to ask the question to Arab Americans in Michigan: How do you feel now about voting for Donald Trump in 2024? I knew it was a stupid thing for you to do in 2024. Was Joe Biden really that much worse than Donald Trump? And did you not have evidence going back to 2015, when Donald Trump tried to push through a Muslim registry in his campaign promise to push through a Muslim registry? Did you have no idea that that's not how this was going to end? Well, it ended that way.

BRZEZINSKI: A lot of people --

SCARBOROUGH: Just like when I see some Hispanics going, "Oh, I can't believe -- I can't believe that he's being so brutal in his deportation tactics," when Donald Trump promised, I believe, in Michigan during the campaign that the mass deportation would be -- and I quote Donald Trump, "bloody" -- a bloody mass deportation. So you voted for him in '24, and you were shocked that he actually did what he said he was going to do in '25. Well, I got to say, in this case, in Michigan, this is just like Ohio. I know Ohio and Michigan. They hate each other. Well, they have one thing in common. The Republican candidates are overreaching. Ramaswamy -- who, from what I understand was Pablo's best friend at Harvard -- Ramaswamy --

PABLO: How dare you?

SCARBOROUGH: -- has overreached.

PABLO: You will hear from my lawyers on that.

SCARBOROUGH: And he's going to pay for that. He just will, most likely, politically -- all the polls suggest that he will pay for that.

PABLO: Yes, he will.

SCARBOROUGH: And then look at Michigan, and it's the same thing here. You know what they could have very easily said? You know what the winning message in Michigan was? "He's one of those DSA guys."

BRZEZINSKI: Yeah.

SCARBOROUGH: "They're going to drive up your taxes -- they're going to pass regulations that are going to cripple Michigan businesses -- they're going to drive people out of the state of Michigan -- you're not going to have a job -- entrepreneurs will never come here -- we've been struggling to rebuild Detroit now for 20 years -- you get a DSA left-wing radical in --" No. Instead, they've gone with a "He's a terrorist -- he's connected to al-Qaeda -- he's connected to Muslim --"

BRZEZINSKI: They've gone Trump.

SCARBOROUGH: People don't believe that. It's like when I first ran, you could have easily said, "He's not smart -- he's a dumb country lawyer -- he's never been in politics." Instead, they attacked me for being a rock star. It was a lie, I swear to God. That was the closing thing. They said, "Oh, he's like a hippie rock star or whatever, going to church 12 days a week." And they overreached. It was stupid. And this overreaching never works.

JONATHAN LEMIRE: And it's emblematic of the Trump era, the Ramaswamy -- who I guess has always been, you know, somewhat sleazy in his personal attacks. But then we see Mike Rogers, who you say did have a good reputation, but he's debased himself because he thinks that's what the politics of the moment calls for -- that that's what Trump expects. He thinks that's what Republican voters want. Well, we're going to find out in a few days if that's true.

SCARBOROUGH: The thing is, he won't even admit that he supports Donald Trump's policies.

LEMIRE: He's trying to have it both ways. ...
news.summary: On Monday's Morning Joe, MS NOW host Joe Scarborough accused Fox News anchor Bret Baier of parroting hate against Abdul el-Sayed and cheered the Michigan Democrat's evasive response to his question about having connections to the Muslim Brotherhood.The MS NOW host went on to taunt Arabs and Hispanics who voted for Donald Trump, calling it a "stupid" thing for them to to do.The segment began with a clip of an interview from Friday's Special Report with Bret Baier in which the Fox host was trying to ask el-Sayed a question about how Michigan Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers was trying to use the Democrat candidate's past support for the Muslim Brotherhood against him.El-Sayed refused to let Baier finish asking his question and suggested that he was not being a "journalist."
