news.title: Everyone says Trump and MAGA are doomed. But Obama's appalling new low and his cabal of Democrat idiots have just tipped this election on its head: MAUREEN CALLAHAN
news.text:
And we thought Michelle was the sellout.

In endorsing Abdul El-Sayed at a Detroit rally on Saturday, Barack Obama has done the unthinkable.

Yes, the one-time kingmaker of the Democratic Party has begun losing his own – and it's symbolic of the absolute chaos engulfing the party.

The mainstream media would have us believe that it's Donald Trump and MAGA on the ropes.

But little attention is paid to the pandemonium on the left, from Congresswoman Ilhan Omar to streamer Hasan Piker to twice-failed Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, who is weighing another White House run in 2028 despite the party begging her not to.

At the moment, it's El-Sayed – and Obama's backing of him – that's causing the most heat.

Multiple Democratic powerbrokers have exclusively told the Daily Mail that they'd rather Republican Mike Rogers defeat El-Sayed, even if that means they fall short of winning control of the Senate.

One source told veteran political journalist and Daily Mail contributor Mark Halperin: 'I don't think Democrats are considering the profound consequences of an El-Sayed win to how the party looks and competes in the 2028 presidential primary.'

Imagine this line-up: El-Sayed vs California Governor Gavin Newsom vs AOC vs Kamala.

It is to weep. Or laugh. Maybe both.

Obama, fresh off castigating black male voters in 2024 for refusing to back Kamala, outright accusing them of misogyny – 'Part of it makes me think that, well, you just aren't feeling the idea of having a woman as president' – is now implying that Dems reluctant to vote for El-Sayed are religious bigots.

This, despite El-Sayed's mother and extended family having been active in the Muslim Brotherhood terrorist group – and that's according to his sister.

Or the pro-Sayed political ad in which a couple shops for groceries, only for the woman to tell her partner to put a carton of eggs back, causing him to ask whether their children don't like them anymore.

'No, they like eggs,' she says. 'But we have to set that $7 aside for killing Palestinians.'

On Monday, El-Sayed's campaign distanced itself, saying the ad was done by the radical left-wing Rebellion PAC.

That's standard procedure for any campaign – disavow a controversial ad and blame the PAC.

The only problem here is that the ad was posted to X by Cenk Uygur, whose nephew and close political associate is Hasan Piker.

The same Piker who campaigned alongside El-Sayed on the eve of his Democratic primary victory.

Lest we forget, Piker once infamously said that 'America deserved 9/11,' – which El-Sayed also disavowed on Meet the Press last August.

'Of course it was a dumb statement,' El-Sayed told host Kristen Welker, though he still refuses to shun Piker. In fact, El-Sayed once called it 'critical' that Dems fulsomely accept him.

Piker, meanwhile, sat in conversation with Ilhan Omar at a sold-out rally in Minneapolis on Tuesday.

Omar is currently under federal investigation for financial misconduct and immigration fraud, the latter allegedly involving Omar marrying her brother. No charges have been filed and Omar has denied the allegations.

Not to mention the major, wide-ranging federal and state investigations into an alleged fraud scheme that paid out billions of dollars in government aid to sham charities in the Somali American community in Democrat-run Minneapolis.

The scale of the scam is so large it may even tip the race for the Minnesota senate seat to Republicans – a rare potential pick-up in a decidedly bad year for the GOP.

At that Tuesday rally, Omar laughed as she said her 'good' looks and charisma were simply too much for Republicans, while Piker blamed – of course – white racism and 'jealousy' for the flashpoint Minneapolis has become.

'White supremacist forces in this country have decided to target Minneapolis because of the successful Somali American community that has been able to thrive here,' he said.

Yes: If there's anything that the United States of America, a nation that prides itself on the assimilation of immigrants from all races and creeds can't stand, it's the success of immigrant communities.

And doesn't all this talk of Minneapolis bring to mind Governor Tim Walz, whose selection by Kamala Harris as her 2024 running mate helped doom her chances?

Walz, who put tampons in boys' school bathrooms? Who was caught in multiple exaggerations, shall we say, of his otherwise meager accomplishments?

Whose wife, Gwen, said in a June 2020 television interview that she kept their windows open during the George Floyd riots, because 'I could smell the burning tires… I kept the windows open as long as I could because I felt like that was such a touchstone of what was happening.'

Back to Omar, whose recent interview with Chris Hayes of MS NOW is a sad yet perfect example of the liberal media's continued, active propagandizing.

As Jonathan Turley at Fox News noted, twelve minutes elapsed before Hayes asked Omar about immigration fraud. Hayes laughed while doing so.

'I am trying to figure out the way to do this,' Hayes said, 'that doesn't sound like I'm insane.'

This is utter journalistic malpractice, the kind that calls to mind the liberal media's insistence that there was nothing cognitively wrong with Joe Biden at all – at all.

Until that fateful debate, which brought us Kamala Harris – who, despite blowing $1 billion and the media's gauzy support, lost to Trump in a blowout that saw black and Hispanic voters voting MAGA.

So why not do it again?

Why not, even as multiple Dem sources told the Daily Mail that Harris has no business running again, and that her statements about possibly doing so have sent the party into 'panic' mode?

'They are repulsed and flabbergasted that she just won't take the hint,' one well-placed source said. Donors, meanwhile, are 'very snarky and condescending' about her chances.

Even her problematic husband, Doug Emhoff, doesn't want her to run again, per a well-sourced report this month in The Wall Street Journal.

So really, who better than Barack Obama, scold of his own party, berating the base for rejecting the mediocrity that was Harris, to insist that Abdul El-Sayed is the guy to 'finish the job'?

Remember: Just two years ago, that was Joe Biden's line.
news.summary: The mainstream media would have us believe that it's Donald Trump and MAGA on the ropes. But little attention is paid to the pandemonium on the left.

news.title: Kamala Harris warns Democrats against third Trump impeachment, urges focus on investigations
news.text: Former US vice president Kamala Harris has urged Democrats against pursuing a third impeachment of President Donald Trump if they regain control of the House of Representatives in next week’s midterm elections, arguing that the party should focus on investigations and holding the administration accountable instead.According to the New York Post, Harris made the remarks during a Tuesday interview with MeidasTouch host Aaron Parnas, saying Democrats had limited resources and should avoid spending them on another impeachment effort.“I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you,” Harris said, adding that the party’s time and resources should be directed towards “accountability” and “investigations”.Harris, who served in the Senate during Trump’s first term and as vice president during his second impeachment trial, also questioned whether Democrats would have enough votes to secure a conviction. “Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-round, and the votes aren’t there,” she said.However, she urged Democrats not to soften their opposition to Trump, calling for an uncompromising approach focused on delivering results after the election. Harris said Democrats should prioritise getting things done rather than engaging in another prolonged political battle.“They’re ruthless, but they’re cruel. And when I say we should be ruthless, I don’t mean cruel, but we should be uncompromising,” she said.Trump was impeached twice during his first term. In December 2019, the Democratic-controlled House impeached him over his dealings with Ukraine, including allegations involving military aid and pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Senate acquitted him in February 2020.In January 2021, the House impeached Trump for a second time, accusing him of inciting the January 6 Capitol riot. The Senate again acquitted him, with Harris serving as vice president during the trial.House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has not ruled out another impeachment effort if Democrats win control of the chamber. He has said the party has “not ruled anything in, and we haven’t ruled anything out”, while indicating that other administration officials, including War Secretary Pete Hegseth, could face scrutiny.Impeachment requires a simple majority in the House, but conviction and removal from office require a two-thirds majority in the Senate.No party has held a two-thirds Senate majority since the mid-1960s, when Democrats briefly controlled 68 of the chamber’s 100 seats.Democratic Representative Al Green of Texas has repeatedly introduced resolutions seeking Trump’s impeachment during his second term, though his efforts have failed to advance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

news.title: The Founder of Arab Americans for Trump Has Some Regrets
news.text:
These attacks have been criticized by Arab and Muslim leaders in Michigan, including Bishara Bahbah, who launched the group Arab Americans for Trump in 2024. That year, he campaigned for the then former President alongside Massad Boulos, the Lebanese businessman who happens to be Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law. I interviewed Bahbah back in August of 2024; we spoke again by phone this week. Our conversation, edited for length and clarity, is below.
Is there anything I should mention to readers about your bio?
I am the chairman of Arab Americans for Peace, and I am still a member of the Republican Party. And I am involved in the current midterm elections.
So, did Arab Americans for Trump become Arab Americans for Peace?
We changed the name last year to Arab Americans for Peace when the President started talking about Gaza as the property of the United States. I believe that Gaza belongs to the Palestinians and no one else, and therefore that kind of talk really was very upsetting and out of line. Therefore, we changed the name.
Didn’t Trump say that Biden has “become like a Palestinian” at the debate in 2024?
He said that about Chuck Schumer.
O.K. He said it about Biden, too.
I released a press release that year saying that the word “Palestinian” is not a slur and it should not be used as such. And it just doesn’t seem to have had an effect because he also recently called Schumer a Palestinian.
You need to keep putting out more statements. Hopefully at some point he’ll understand that it’s offensive. But I want to talk about what’s happening in the Michigan Senate race right now, because you said you’re still a Republican, and what’s happening, as far as I can tell, is that Abdul El-Sayed is running against Mike Rogers and is facing a tremendous amount of bigotry and Islamophobia from the Rogers campaign and its surrogates and from President Trump. How bad has it gotten?
I’m going to Michigan on Wednesday, and I’m a Christian. I’m not even a Muslim, but the fact that Muslims are being targeted in such a demeaning, racist fashion is just crossing a red line, like calling him “Muhammad.” We know that Muhammad is widely considered the most popular name in the world. Would the President like to be called something other than Mr. President or Donald J. Trump? Is it acceptable for somebody else to come up with a different name and call him that just because they would like to do so? It’s not. So Islam and Islamophobia is going to only have a counter-effect with regard to the Arab and Muslim voters in the United States and also voters who are levelheaded because bigotry is just not acceptable.
And I think the fact that the President is escalating his attacks along those lines is a sign of desperation.
But even when Trump has not been desperate—and it seems like he might be a little desperate now, since Republicans seem like they’re about to have a bad election—Trump’s bigotry and attacks on minority groups, including Muslims, have been constant. This is not just that his party’s behind in the Michigan Senate race, so he’s going to launch a few broadsides against Muslims. This is his entire political career, no?
Well, in 2024, the President seemed to have behaved.
Sir, I just said to you that he called Joe Biden a Palestinian during the debate.
I understand that. I understand that. I’m not questioning that either. All I’m saying is that his tone during the elections in 2024 was very different than what it is right now. He said something at one point in 2024 that offended the Yemenis in Michigan, and he immediately apologized.
Oh, he apologized?
He apologized at the time, yes. [Amer Ghalib, the mayor of Hamtramck, Michigan, who supported Trump in 2024, claims that Trump apologised privately for calling Yemenis “terrorists” but added that Trump declined to do so publicly.] But it seems like in 2024 the President was desperate to get the Arab and Muslim vote.
He made lots of racist comments during 2024. He talked about Haitians eating pets.

So when you said that he behaved during 2024, I just wasn’t sure what you meant.
I mean, it was not to the extent that it is right now. And he attacked the Somalis, he attacked the Haitians, and that’s not acceptable.
O.K. But it’s gotten worse now, you’re saying?
It’s gotten a lot worse, yes.
So it’s like if there was a list, the Muhammad thing would be at the top of the list, and then the Haitian stuff and the Somali stuff would be a little lower down the list.
Well, I mean, they’re all offensive. And I wouldn’t say that, because I’m Arab American, I’m more offended by the Muhammad issue. It is just all equally offensive. I feel bad for the Haitians, for the Somalis, for the Palestinians, for the Muslims. It is just not acceptable.
A number of Muslim Americans either voted for Trump or did not vote for Kamala Harris. And one of the main reasons was the devastation that was going on in Gaza, that the Biden Administration had supported. And I think a lot of liberal people were angry when people didn’t vote for Kamala, but a lot of people also felt that what was happening in Gaza was unconscionable. That was part of what you were thinking, correct?
Absolutely. I mean, our priority in 2024 was to end the war in Gaza, and our pleas with the Democrats at the time went nowhere. And President Trump, at the time, promised that he would end the war in Gaza. [During the debate with Biden in June of 2024, Trump also urged Biden to let Israel “finish the job” in Gaza.]
I think your critique of the Democratic Party is one that a lot of people have become more and more sympathetic to over the past few years. But when I talked to you last time it wasn’t your critique of the Democratic Party on Gaza that I found so surprising. It was that you seemed to be putting personal and political trust in Donald Trump, and I think that’s the part that people find a little hard to wrap their minds around.
You’re right. You’re right. I had faith. I believed his words. And now, on the Gaza situation, well, we were able to get a ceasefire in Gaza, and you might have heard or read that I was personally involved in the negotiations leading up to the ceasefire in Gaza, beginning with my intervention on behalf of the White House as a background negotiator between Hamas and the White House. [Asked for comment about Bahbah’s claims, a Trump Administration official told The New Yorker, “None of this is accurate. This individual was not involved in peace negotiations between Israel and Hamas.”]
The ceasefire that happened in January of 2025, or the ceasefire in October of 2025?
Well, both. There was a ceasefire that was forced upon Netanyahu by Trump in January of 2025. Then, in March of 2025, Netanyahu was able to convince the President that he had to finish the job, meaning finish Hamas, and broke his word with regard to the ceasefire.
And then proceeded to cut off aid to Gaza for months.
Let me tell you the way things have transpired from my perspective. So, in March of 2025, Netanyahu was able to convince Trump to allow him to break the ceasefire and resume the fighting, which led to famine in Gaza during the summer of 2025. After that, I was asked by [the United States special envoy to the Middle East Steve] Witkoff to get involved in the negotiations with regard to the ceasefire in Gaza. And the initial Witkoff proposal that was made public then was a proposal that I had written for Witkoff. So we got engaged in the ceasefire negotiations, which really took a very long time and ended up in another ceasefire in October of 2025. So there were two ceasefires at the time, and now, of course, the ceasefire of October 2025 was supposed to go into phases, and it led to the release of the Israeli hostages, and it led to the release of the Palestinian hostages in return.
You said earlier that you changed the name of the organization when he said that Gaza belonged to the United States, correct? That happened in February of 2025. But you were still working with the Trump Administration well after this, correct?
Yes. I was asked by Witkoff to mediate between Hamas and the White House.
You were communicating with Witkoff, and you also campaigned with Massad Boulos, who is Tiffany Trump’s father-in-law. And these are people that you have real relationships with, I assume. What do they say now? Are you still in touch with them?
No, I’m not in touch with Massad Boulos. Our relationship ended right after the elections.
Which elections?
After the Presidential elections. He just cut off communication, and all the promises that were made with regard to what the President would do for the Arab American community were never really fulfilled. And Massad Boulos essentially cut off the relationship with me.
He just didn’t respond to messages, that type of thing?
No. One of the things that Mossad Boulos reportedly did was meet with the head of the Regional Council of Judea and Samaria. And he called him Governor. Governor of what? A governor of the West Bank, which is an occupied territory. That, to me, was a reason to sever ties with Massad Boulos because—
Oh, so you’re the one who severed ties?
I severed the ties.
You say you’re still a Republican. Does that mean you’re still hoping for Republican success, but not in Michigan? How are you thinking about what you’re rooting for in these elections?
Well, as far as I’m concerned, community comes first before the Party, and the country comes before the Party and community. So this is where I stand right now.
Where is where you stand?
Community comes first before the Party.
So you’re not hoping Republicans win in 2026?
Well, all I’m saying is that the rhetoric that has been lobbed against our community has turned off the community, and I don’t see the community voting Republican this time around.
But what about you? How are you going to vote?
I’m not going to answer that question.
O.K. Do you think that some people might think that the stand you’re taking against Trump and his bigotry now is slightly undermined by not even saying that you believe people should vote for the opponents of Trump and that bigotry?
People can interpret what I’m saying any way they want, and that’s fine with me. All I’m saying is our support of Trump in 2024 was for the primary and sole reason of ending the war in Gaza. That was it. It was not necessarily . . . I mean, a lot of the values of the Republican Party match with the values of the Arab and Muslim American voters, which is fine, but sometimes there is a breaking point because when there is no respect for the community, how is the community going to behave? I mean, the community is not dumb. They expect to vote for people who support them. They’re not to be expected to vote for people who attack them.
When I look back at our previous interview, it’s a lot of me asking you questions about things Trump said, and you essentially denying them or saying that he’s been misunderstood, or essentially that it won’t be that bad, or it was so great because you got on a phone call with Trump.
I did say those things.
And do you feel like you were vying for influence, and so you had to say them? Do you feel like you were a little bit brainwashed and you actually thought that Trump was a different person? How do you understand looking back?
Well, I was counting on his commitment to end the war in Gaza. That was my primary reason.
Right. And I’m asking why you believed it.
He told me that in person multiple times. I mean, he told the whole country that he demanded—
Sir, you must know Donald Trump saying something, whether it’s to you in person or to the country, has no meaning, right? You know that.
Well, he told the entire country that he’s a man of peace, that he has not waged any wars during his time, and that he wants to bring about peace in the world. And, honestly, I believed him at the time.
Right. I believe that you said something about him being a President who ends wars, and I had to remind you that Joe Biden had ended the war in Afghanistan. Trump actually increased drone strikes. You seemed to be of the opinion that Trump was much more of a man of peace than perhaps the record suggested. That’s why I’m asking these questions.
If you’re asking that I had put too much faith in President Trump at the time, I did. If you’re asking me if I had believed his words at the time with regard to the ceasefire in Gaza, I did. If I was misled, I was misled along with the entire country.
I guess there were also a lot of people in the country who were horrified by what was happening in Gaza and were angry about it, but also never put any faith in Donald Trump. And it seems like that position has been somewhat vindicated.
We’re all different in terms of how we react to people and statements, but at the same time the fact that I knew that in his first term he imposed the Muslim ban, and then when we asked him about it during 2024, he said, “No, no, no, there’s not going to be a Muslim ban, and there’s not going to be wars.” Unfortunately, it seems to me that maybe I was too naïve at the time.
I know I’ve asked you a version of this before, but just to try to reflect on it, when you do think back to those days when you were campaigning with Massad Boulos, campaigning for Trump, talking to him on the phone, what do you think about that now? What pops into your mind?
I did what I did for Gaza, and Biden did not listen to us, and a wise individual should make a choice between a bad situation and a worse situation, and I was forced to make that type of a choice.
And do you think you made the right choice?
Well, we ended the war in Gaza. It’s not a perfect ceasefire right now because there are people who are getting killed by the Israelis on a daily basis, and the United States is not saying a word about those violations. And, also, you look at what’s happening in the West Bank, which is being literally overtaken by extremist Jewish settlers who are doing whatever they want to do with the acquiescence of the Israeli Army and the Israeli government, and without any objection from the U.S. government. So I am terribly disappointed in what has transpired, and given that I’m that disappointed, I don’t really hold much hope for the coming two years as far as anything happening with regard to Gaza. ♦
news.summary: As the President and his party launch a wave of bigoted attacks on Abdul El-Sayed, Bishara Bahbah reflects on what, exactly, Trump has delivered in his second term.
news.author: Isaac Chotiner

news.title: MAGA Nepo Senator Hit by Shock Poll Just Days Before Election
news.text:
Lindsey Graham’s sister risks throwing away the late MAGA Senator’s Republican stronghold seat.

Nepo Senator Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews are tied at 48 percent in South Carolina’s deep-red Senate race, according to a stunning new New York Times/Siena poll released Wednesday.

The state last elected a Democratic senator in 1998, when it backed Fritz Hollings, who had held the seat since 1966.

Asked who the 707 respondents would vote for if the election were held now, both candidates came out with 48 percent of the vote. 

This included 7 percent of people who identified as Republican who said they planned to swing to Andrews, as well as 8 percent of people who voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election. Just two percent of Kamala Harris voters said they were backing Graham.

According to the new numbers, 57 percent of Independents said they planned to back Andrews compared to just 37 percent who said they planned to back Graham. 

Graham took over from her brother following his sudden death in July from a rare cardiovascular disease, but has since raised eyebrows with her credentials and shaky media performances. 

The 62-year-old enjoys a higher profile than Andrews, whom almost a quarter of respondents said they’d never heard of. 

The Daily Beast has contacted Graham’s team for comment. 

Lindsey Graham became a leading figure in the MAGA movement, known for his hawkish stance on foreign policy and as a major advocate of projecting American strength through force and interventionism. 

He played a central role in securing equipment and munitions for Ukraine in its fight against Russia. He was also a leading advocate for starting a war with Iran. 

It comes as the GOP faces a broader blue wave across the nation, as America prepares to pass judgment on a historically unpopular president. Trump has overseen soaring gas and grocery prices and started a new war in the Middle East that has no end in sight, has cost $47.1 billion, and has claimed the lives of 18 U.S. service members. 

The GOP’s predicament has forced it to spend time and money trying to shore up voters in parts of the country it would usually be able to rely on. 

Trump has also taken breaks from his presidential duties to tour the country in a bid to woo his base, including in South Carolina, amid fears that his absence from the ballot will lead to a drop in MAGA turnout. 

Seventy-three percent of South Carolina respondents said they were at least somewhat likely to vote next week.

Nepo Senator Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews are tied at 48 percent in South Carolina’s deep-red Senate race, according to a stunning new New York Times/Siena poll released Wednesday.

The state last elected a Democratic senator in 1998, when it backed Fritz Hollings, who had held the seat since 1966.

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Democrat's 2-word answer on a possible presidential run draws cheers from Maine crowd
news.text: Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., appeared to leave the door open for a presidential run in 2028 while giving a stump speech on Tuesday for Troy Jackson, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Maine. Kelly was in the middle of an argument about how the economy no longer works for young Americans when an audience member interrupted him with a suggestion about his political future. "I'm the son of two cops who went to public schools and went on to become a Navy pilot and then an astronaut and now a U.S. senator. I was fortunate," he said. Just as Kelly mentioned becoming a senator, someone in the crowd shouted "president," prompting a two-word response from the Arizona Democrat. WATCH: DEM SENATORS DODGE BACKING KAMALA HARRIS IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN: ‘VERY MESSY’ "We'll see," said Kelly, whose short response drew cheers from the crowd. Kelly, who is up for re-election in 2028, is routinely featured in 2028 Democratic presidential primary surveys and often polls below more established contenders like former Vice President Kamala Harris and California Gov. Gavin Newsom. Still, Kelly has begun gaining support as his national profile rises. He drew widespread attention in Nov. 2025 after appearing in a video alongside other Democratic lawmakers telling U.S. service members that it is their duty to disobey illegal orders, including those issued by the executive branch. The video prompted a criminal investigation into Kelly and the five other Democratic lawmakers, although a federal grand jury declined to indict them in February. HARRIS KEEPS 2028 DOOR OPEN AS SHE HITS MIDTERM CAMPAIGN TRAIL, WARNS ‘28 WON’T MATTER’ WITHOUT 2026 Axios reported last week that Kelly is eyeing a run for the White House. He told the outlet that he will decide whether he is running for president or another term in the Senate after the midterms. However, Kelly would not necessarily have to choose between the two. Under Arizona law, presidential and vice presidential candidates are permitted to simultaneously seek election to one additional federal office, meaning Kelly could run for both president and Senate in 2028. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The provision in Arizona law could make a presidential bid less of a political gamble for Kelly, allowing him to pursue the highest office in the land without necessarily jeopardizing his Senate career. If Kelly secures the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028, he could appear on Arizona ballots as a candidate for both president and the Senate, though he wouldn't be able to occupy both offices if he won both races.
news.summary: Mark Kelly responded "we'll see" when an audience member shouted "president" during a stump speech, fueling 2028 presidential election speculation.

news.title: Black Celebrities Push Voter Engagement Ahead of the Midterms
news.text:
If you’re tired of politicians and skeptical that your vote counts, you’re not alone. But with so much at stake, this election cycle is one we can’t afford to sit out. With only days left until the 2026 midterm elections, many Black celebrities are sounding the alarm and urging their fans to get out and make their voices heard.

From Jayda Cheaves’ personal reckoning with the ballot box to Rihanna’s thoughts on non-voters, the message is sparking a bigger conversation about power, accountability and who pays the price when we disengage.

Jayda Cheaves Votes for the First Time in Years

Influencer Jayda Cheaves is keeping it real about political disillusionment and why she decided to vote after missing out on recent elections. “I made it my business this year to vote,” she said in an Instagram story, explaining that her grandmother’s warning and her own research pushed her to act. Cheaves said she didn’t vote in the 2024 election because “There’s no way they’re letting a Black woman [former Democratic nominee and Vice President Kamala Harris] be president, so why would I waste my time?”

Now, her message has changed. “You need to vote,” she stressed. ”It’s important.”

RELATED: Black Women Are Preparing for the Midterms Over This Sunday Brunch

Monaleo Endorses James Talarico

When it comes to young entertainers leading the charge for political engagement, Houston rapper Monaleo is at the top of the list. She recently took her voting message directly to students at Texas Southern University, joining Texas Senate candidate James Talarico’s campaign stop. “After we vote, we need to tell everybody else to get up and go vote,” she urged, calling on Gen Z to turn social media influence into real-world turnout.

John Legend Returns Home to Ohio

Grammy-winning singer and Ohio native John Legend’s civic influence is rooted in years of political engagement and public advocacy. He joined Democratic candidates Sherrod Brown and Dr. Amy Acton at a rally on October 26. His appearance brought star power to a high-stakes campaign focused on affordability and public services.

“In eight days, the nation will be watching Ohio. And when the nation sees us this time, it won’t be about some poisonous slander hurled into the headlines,” Legend said. 

Marsai Martin Encourages Gen-Z to Stand Up

We previously told you that actor and producer Marsai Martin is part of a generation of young Black creatives who have been using their voices to reach first-time voters. 

“My first vote taught me something I didn’t expect: participating is contagious,” she wrote in Teen Vogue. “When one person makes it feel normal and important, the people around them are more likely to get involved too.”

Kendrick Sampson Challenges Celebrity Politics

Actor and organizer Kendrick Sampson joined Houston’s “The Power of Showing Up” forum, where community members examined what voting must accomplish beyond Election Day. He challenged celebrity politics without community accountability, stressing mutual care and sustained organizing. For him, voting matters, but the work cannot stop at the ballot box. He told the audience that Black people in positions of power don’t always act in the community’s best interest.

“We can’t expect Black faces in high places,” Sampson said, according to The Defender. “Usually, Black faces in high places got to that high place because they compromised to get close to white people.” 

Jenifer Lewis Uses Music to Reach Voters

Actress Jenifer Lewis is using music, humor and sisterhood to cut through election fatigue. In a recent video with prominent Black women, she leads a blunt refrain: “Get your ass out and vote.” The “Women Like Us” campaign points people to Vote.org, making a nonpartisan push for participation, rather than a candidate endorsement.

Piles Warns About a Plan to Disengage Black Voters

When it comes to voting, rapper Piles is questioning how and why Black Americans have been persuaded that voting does not matter. On social media, he’s stressing the important history of Black Americans voting while also reflecting on Barack Obama and Kamala Harris’s historic candidacies.

He said enthusiasm among Black voters can affect elections. “I’ll NEVER Allow This Country To EVER Fool Me Again,” he tweeted. “I Don’t Fight B/c I Believe In What America Is Selling. I Fight B/c They Hope I GIVE UP!!!”

Tasha Smith Stresses Civic Engagement

Actor and director Tasha Smith joined Jenifer Lewis and other Black women in a musical appeal urging Americans to vote in the midterms. The campaign’s direct, memorable message is designed to reach people tired of political noise. Her participation adds a recognizable entertainment voice to a collective, nonpartisan call for civic engagement.

Gail Bean and the Get Out the Vote Campaign

Actor Gail Bean was also among the Black women who joined Jenifer Lewis’s musical get-out-the-vote appeal. The group’s refrain, “This ain’t the election to sit home and lurk,” turns voter participation into a shared responsibility. Bean’s involvement helps carry that message through entertainment culture.

Danielle Pinnock Joins Black Women for Voting Rights

NAACP Image Award winner and actress also lent her voice to Jenifer Lewis’s collective midterm voting appeal. The campaign uses humor, music and recognizable Black women to challenge voter apathy, while directing audiences to Vote.org for practical information. Her participation reminds us that civic engagement should be a community effort, not a solo act.

David Banner Wants Politicians to Tell the Truth

Rapper and activist David Banner told the audience at Houston’s “The Power of Showing Up” forum that voting must be matched by accountability. “Although we do need to vote,” he said, candidates must be willing to explain what they will do for Black communities.

“The problem is most people who are running are too afraid to tell you what they’re going to do for your community,” he said. “They tell every other subsection in America exactly what they’re going to do.”

Rihanna Calls Out Non-Voters

Rihanna is calling out voter apathy after weighing in on a viral discussion about Trump’s 2024 reelection. 

“And believe it or not, those who didn’t vote at all also did this!” she wrote on Instagram, arguing that non-voters also share responsibility for the outcome of the last presidential election. The Barbadian superstar continues using her platform to spark conversations about civic participation.
news.summary:
Rihanna, Jenifer Lewis and Piles are among the Black stars challenging voter apathy and reminding folks what’s at stake ahead of the midterm elections.

news.title: Must-Win Republican’s New Ad Gets Brutal Verdict From Ex-Aide
news.text:
Republican Sen. Susan Collins has made a colossal campaign blunder that one of her former staffers says may well have cost the GOP a must-win election.

Collins’ team put out a 30-second spot featuring Maine TV personality Bill Green talking the senator up and taking aim at her Democratic opponent Troy Jackson over his background as a logger.

“Now, I also know Troy Jackson, but we’re not talking about buying a cord of wood here,” Green says in the ad. “We’re sending someone to the U.S. Senate, and Troy doesn’t have the tools he needs to be effective.”

Collins’ ex-aide Sam Patten led the online backlash by torching the incumbent for going after Jackson’s blue-collar roots.

“I didn’t believe this ad was real,” Patten wrote. “For more than 30 years, Susan Collins has carefully concealed her intrinsic arrogance because she is very smart and knows well that in Maine politics that would be fatal.”

“With this ad, she gave that up,” he went on. “The race is over.”

He wasn’t alone. Democratic former congressional candidate Jordan Wood said the commercial “made my jaw drop,” while labor federation Maine AFL-CIO said that “Susan Collins has spent so much time in Washington she thinks working-class Mainers are beneath her.”

Collins, 73, is a multimillionaire whose family has operated a lumber business in northern Maine since 1844. 

Jackson, 58, a former logger who went on to become president of the Maine Senate, has built his campaign around attacking Collins as out of touch with ordinary Mainers struggling with unaffordability under Donald Trump. 

The incumbent first won election in 1996. She has spent nearly three decades cultivating a reputation as an independent-minded moderate in the purple state and lately as one of the few Republicans willing to challenge the president’s MAGA agenda. 

Her bid for a sixth term has now descended into a bruising fight for survival in a state that backed Kamala Harris over Trump in 2024. 

Collins’ campaign was already in trouble before her latest commercial aired, with polls putting Jackson ahead by 2 percentage points among likely voters and the Cook Political Report rating the contest a toss-up. 

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, meaning Democrats need to gain a net four seats to seize control of the chamber at the midterm elections next Tuesday.

The Daily Beast has contacted Collins’ campaign for comment on this story.

news.title: US midterms: Six days left – who leads in the polls as Trump, Obama rally  - Dominican Republic Post –
news.text:
President Donald Trump has stepped up his campaigning, holding two Republican rallies in Texas on Tuesday before heading to Ohio on Wednesday. Ex-President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris are also hitting the campaign trail in Georgia for the Democratic Party.

Here is what the latest polls say, what happened on the campaign trail and what to expect on Wednesday.

What do the latest polls suggest?

With less than a week to go before the midterms, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests the Democrats are ahead of the Republicans by nine points.

According to the October 22-26 survey, 47 percent of voters support the Democrats, compared with 36 percent who support the Republicans. When undecided voters’ leanings were taken into account, Democrats lead with 50 percent compared with Republicans’ 41 percent.

Trump’s approval rating improved by a percentage point to 32 percent, with 73 percent of US adults saying the cost of living was going in the wrong direction.

In Texas, where Democrats have not won a Senate election since 1988, James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are virtually tied in the polls.

Trump has made several trips to the state ahead of the midterms, but the polls indicate a much tighter race than the president has suggested.

“The good people of Texas have probably never seen so much of President Trump. Four visits in seven weeks, which, to put that into context, is twice as many as we saw at the comparable period leading up to the 2024 election, which perhaps shows just how concerned Republicans are,” Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle said, reporting from the Texas coastal city of Corpus Christi.

Lavelle said local analysis suggested more Republicans have voted early than Democrats, but Talarico has also been courting Republicans dissatisfied with Trump.

“That doesn’t mean Republicans are voting for Republican candidates,” Lavelle said.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are also competing in a closely contested Senate race.

“I was a Republican forever, but I became an independent in the last two elections,” Michael Alexander, a Native American backing El-Sayed, told Al Jazeera.

“I don’t really vote for a party any more. I vote for who I think will do the best job.”

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but Republican incumbent Roger Marshall now faces a close contest against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

The race has brought Trump and his deputy, JD Vance, to the state.

“There’s a reason why we’re seeing not only US President Donald Trump but also Vice President JD Vance heading to Kansas because it’s actually in play,” Al Jazeera’s Patty Culhane said.

According to The Associated Press news agency, both parties and their allied groups have committed about $71m to campaign advertising in the Kansas race, making it the most expensive Senate contest in the state’s history.

What happened in the US midterm campaigns over the past 24 hours?

Trump addressed two campaign rallies in Texas on Tuesday in support of Paxton.

In Corpus Christi, Trump pointed to a tanker that he said was carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan oil and called it a win for his administration. He also suggested the idea of making Venezuela the 51st US state. The Trump administration has signed an oil deal with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodriguez, after abducting socialist President Nicolas Maduro in a military operation in January.

Trump also announced plans to roll back the Biden-era restrictions on methane emissions from oil and gas production, stating that it would help bring down energy prices.

Fuel prices have become a huge election issue as the US-Israel war on Iran continues. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also joined Trump for a rare campaign-trail appearance in Texas.

In Alaska, Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski has backed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins for governor rather than Bernadette Wilson, the Trump-endorsed candidate.

What’s next for Democrats and Republicans on Wednesday?

Trump heads to Ohio on Wednesday for his third rally in the state this month, as Republicans try to defend a Senate seat being challenged by former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.

The US president is scheduled to speak in Chillicothe at 23:00 GMT. Republican Senator Jon Husted, who took over Vance’s seat when he became vice president, is facing Brown, who is seeking a return to the Senate after losing his seat in 2024.

The two are in a closely contested race, with more than $400m spent or reserved for campaign advertising as of October 8, according to an Axios report.

Republicans are particularly concerned in Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa, where even a few percentage points for a third party could swing the outcome.

Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Ohio on Wednesday and Iowa on Sunday.

Vance will be in Kinston, North Carolina, campaigning for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper. The vice president is expected to speak at 16:30 GMT.

In Georgia, former President Obama will campaign in Atlanta alongside Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms at 20:00 GMT.

Ossoff is running against Republican Mike Collins, while Bottoms faces Republican Rick Jackson in the governor’s race. Trump won Georgia in the 2024 presidential election.

Former Vice President Harris also begins a three-day visit to Georgia on Wednesday, with early in-person voting due to end on Friday, October 30.

In Wisconsin, Marquette Law School will publish its latest statewide poll at 18:15 GMT.

Wednesday’s poll will also examine voters’ views on inflation, tariffs, the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s presidency.

news.title: US Midterms: Six Days to Go – Poll Leaders as Trump and Obama Campaign
news.text:
With just six days remaining until the midterm elections in the United States on November 3, Democrats are currently leading Republicans in national polls, though several critical Senate races are too close to call. 

President Donald Trump intensified his campaigning this week, holding two rallies in Texas on Tuesday before heading to Ohio on Wednesday. Meanwhile, former President Barack Obama and ex-Vice President Kamala Harris are actively campaigning for the Democratic Party in Georgia.

Recent polling indicates that Democrats have a nine-point advantage over Republicans, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey conducted from October 22 to 26. The poll shows 47% of voters supporting Democrats, compared to 36% for Republicans. When factoring in undecided voters, the Democratic lead rises to 50% against 41% for the Republicans. Trump’s approval rating ticked up to 32%, although 73% of Americans believe the cost of living is headed in the wrong direction.

In Texas, a traditionally Republican stronghold where Democrats haven’t won a Senate seat since 1988, the race between James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton is virtually tied. Trump has made multiple visits to Texas in the lead-up to the elections, yet polls suggest a tighter competition than he has portrayed. Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle reported that local analysis shows a higher number of early Republican voters, but Talarico is appealing to dissatisfied Trump voters.

In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are locked in a closely contested race. Michael Alexander, a voter who shifted from Republican to independent, remarked, “I don’t really vote for a party anymore. I vote for who I think will do the best job.”

Kansas is experiencing a competitive Senate race for the first time since 1932, as Republican incumbent Roger Marshall faces a challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. Both parties have committed around $71 million for campaign advertising in what is now the state’s costliest Senate contest.

In Texas, Trump addressed supporters during his rallies, touting a deal involving Venezuelan oil and his intention to roll back methane emission regulations to ease energy prices. Fuel costs have emerged as a significant election issue amid ongoing conflicts in the region.

On Wednesday, Trump will rally in Ohio, defending a Senate seat against former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. The contest is tight, with over $400 million directed towards campaign ads as of early October. 

Republicans face challenges in Texas, Ohio, Kansas, and Iowa, where small shifts in voter preference could significantly impact outcomes. Besides Trump, Vice President JD Vance will campaign in North Carolina for Republican candidate Michael Whatley. Meanwhile, Obama and Harris will collaborate on a campaign effort in Georgia alongside local Democratic candidates.

On Friday, early in-person voting will conclude in Georgia, while Wisconsin’s Marquette Law School is set to release a new statewide poll examining public sentiment on inflation and various political issues.

news.title: Congresswoman: If Democrats Win Power, What Will We Do With It? | Opinion
news.text: If the polling and news chatter are correct, Democrats are on the verge of a historic win in the House and potentially the Senate. We are winning. But when the time comes, what will we do with the governing power? The polls have been clear: voters across the country are using our democratic process to express their discontent with an economy that's failing them and are turning away from Trump. Progressive victories point to the frustration felt across the country. Voters may give us a mandate, and the question is: what will we do with it? Returning to the status quo will not be enough. Voters will not be patient with excuses, nor will they be satisfied with the adage "that's just not how things get done.” If we fail to really address the concerns that keep voters up at night, we risk reinforcing the belief that the system doesn’t work and that nothing in Washington ever really changes. History doesn't necessarily repeat itself, but it sure does inform. In 2020, President Biden won, but economic anxiety continued to fuel voter dissatisfaction throughout his term. By 2024, Kamala Harris’ insistence that there was little daylight between her and Biden only reinforced the sense among many voters that all they could expect was more of the same. I saw that frustration firsthand. As co-director of a national network of grassroots organizations that engaged voters before and after the 2024 election, the number one issue expressed at doors was the sense that the economic anxieties of everyday people were invisible to those in power. Renters were struggling with the housing crisis but only heard proposals around homeownership. Seniors on fixed incomes worried about losing ground with ever-rising costs. Young people were increasingly uncertain that they could build a better future. And as a result, in 2024, a shocking 90 million people stayed home for the election. While not all of them would have voted for Harris, analysis shows that disengagement played a major role in the outcome. If voters hand Democrats power on November 3, they will expect us to use it. Voters will rightfully expect accountability and action. For many, tackling the affordability crisis begins with lowering costs at the gas pump and grocery store. Ending this illegal war will be a key factor in achieving that. For others, fighting the culture of corruption and stopping billionaires from further raiding public coffers is top of mind. What's more, my fellow Democrats will be best served if we remember that addressing the affordability crisis is not just about lowering costs; it's about putting more money in people’s pockets. That’s why I proposed raising the minimum wage to $25 an hour, because there isn’t a place in America where you can live on $7.25. Far from out of touch, these proposals carry strong support. Recent polling shows 66 percent of Americans support a national health plan, 76 percent say health care should be guaranteed as a right, and 75 percent worry about food affordability, while 83 percent say tariffs raise prices. A September Wall Street Journal poll also found bipartisan support for capping drug prices and credit card interest rates and restricting institutional investors from buying single-family homes. The American people are not afraid of bold ideas. They are hungry for them. That is the lesson I took from my own election, where even in a special election held on a Thursday in April, 136,000 people turned out. We must recognize that organized people can beat organized money. And since my race in New Jersey, we have seen that lesson play out across the country as progressive candidates have won primaries up and down the ballot. Voters are practically begging us to reject politics as usual. But winning differently only matters if we are willing to govern differently. Six months in Congress have taught me that winning an election is not enough. We have to be willing to fight for the people who sent us here, even when the establishment tells us we can’t. If voters give us governing power, then we have to govern. Democrats across the ideological spectrum should be prepared to put a popular agenda on the president’s desk and dare him to veto it. Make him explain why billionaires deserve another tax break while working families struggle. For too long, Washington has taught politicians to think about power as something to hold rather than something to use. In the short time I've served, I’ve learned that far too many politicians view survival as an individual endeavor. Protect your seat. Protect your title. Protect your donors. Don’t rock the boat. Do just enough without upsetting the apple cart. But that’s not what our voters want, and it sure won’t change the lives of any of our constituents. In the richest country in the world, working people are choosing between groceries and rent, splitting pills to make prescriptions last, and sending their children to school in shoes with holes, all while we spend billions on an endless war that nobody wants. This is not the moment for cowardice. This November, voters may put their faith in Democrats again. We should understand what that faith means. It is not permission to go back to business as usual. It is a demand that we stand up to MAGA extremism and use the power voters give us to materially improve their lives. We cannot ask people to save democracy every two years while giving them a government they do not believe can change their lives. If voters entrust us with power, our responsibility is to use it. And if we expect voters not only to elect us in November but to keep us in power for the long haul, we have to give them a reason to believe their vote changed something. Democrats cannot just stand by. I sure as hell won’t. Analilia Mejia represents New Jersey's 11th District. The views expressed in this article are the writer’s own.
news.summary: "Democrats need to deliver if we want to keep the Congress for the long haul."
news.author: Analilia Mejia

news.title: Democrats target a 'flippable' Senate seat in the Milwaukee suburbs
news.text:
MADISON – If Wisconsin's state Senate is the "most flippable" legislative chamber in the country, the 5th District has been presented as its "most flippable" seat since Democrats launched their campaign efforts more than a year ago.

State Rep. Robyn Vining, D-Wauwatosa, was one of the first two Democratic candidates to announce Senate bids with the party's backing last summer for the second set of elections on new, more competitive legislative maps. Democrats picked up four seats in 2024 despite the party's presidential candidate, Kamala Harris, losing at the top the ticket.

More: All of our voters guide stories to key Wisconsin legislative races

"The path to the Democratic majority, the path to fully funding our public schools, the path to fighting back against gun violence with meaningful reforms, the path to quality, affordable health care and mental healthcare and childcare runs straight through the 5th Senate District," Vining told supporters when she announced her campaign last summer.

Six months after Vining launched her campaign, Sen. Rob Hutton, R-Brookfield, said he would not seek reelection, and GOP candidate and founder of Wisconsin Orthopedic Physical Therapy Mike Roberts entered the race, citing his experience as a health care provider and business owner as a driving force behind his campaign.

"I go in the treatment room, I develop relationships, I talk to people. More importantly, I listen to them," Roberts told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel. "That's what I've done for my entire career – hearing what their problems are and finding solutions. So honestly, [the campaign] hasn't been a whole lot different."

Since then, the district has been a target for both parties – but it has taken a back seat to others they see as more competitive, like the 17th and 21st Districts in the state's southwestern and southeastern corners of the state, respectively.

"We're feeling cautiously optimistic," Senate Minority Leader Dianne Hesselbein, D-Middleton, told the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel.

The 5th Senate District encompasses communities west of Milwaukee running from Pewaukee through Brookfield, into Wauwatosa and West Allis.

It broke for Harris over Republican President Donald Trump by 5.9 points in the fall 2024 election, for liberal state Supreme Court Justice Susan Crawford by 13.5 points in the spring of that year and for liberal Justice Chris Taylor by 17.8 points in spring 2026.

Vining, a photographer and former pastor, made her entrance to the Assembly by flipping a district. She narrowly defeated her Republican opponent in 2018 in a traditionally GOP district once held by former Gov. Scott Walker.

"I have always run campaigns on shared values," Vining told the Journal Sentinel.

Her campaign messaging includes merchandise and signs with the slogan "Love Wins," which she first wrote on a sign she carried protesting Walker's Act 10 legislation at the state Capitol in 2011 as "a rejection of 'divide and conquer' politics."

"'Divide and conquer' politics is is bad for human beings. It's bad for our mental health. It's bad for our relationships, communities, neighborhoods," she said.

Roberts, who partnered with his wife to open his physical therapy clinic in 2013, struck a similar tone, noting he treats patients of all political stripes.

"Both sides of the aisle are at fault for this," Roberts said. "Republicans and Democrats. This is what I've heard from thousands of patients. They're sick and tired of the political divide. … They want someone that's going to actually listen to their constituents and work across the aisle."

Constituents in the 5th Senate District and throughout the state "deserve a problem solver," Roberts said.

Roberts has been "a star candidate in a district that is probably, on paper, one of the toughest ones for us to hold," Sen. Patrick Testin, R-Stevens Point, told the Journal Sentinel.

Testin, who is leading the Committee to Elect a Republican Senate's efforts this fall, applauded Roberts for running a strong campaign, knocking doors and raising money despite the district's leftward tilt.

"It's still going to be an uphill battle in that seat," Testin said.

The district "started moving in the wrong direction [for Republicans], even going back to 2018," Testin said, pointing to Republican former Sen. Dale Kooyenga's narrow victory that year over Democrat Julie Henzsey.

Kooyenga, who now leads the Metropolitan Milwaukee Association of Commerce, won by 2.4 points to serve in the seat vacated by Republican Leah Vukmir in her run for U.S. Senate. The district has not been represented by a Democrat since 2010, when Vukmir ousted Democrat Jim Sullivan.

"A lot of it is the the suburbs and places like Wauwatosa and Brookfield that once were bedrocks for conservative voters that, since Donald Trump took the Oval Office back in 2016, we've seen those areas of the state sort of move in a a different direction," Testin said.

Campaign committees focused on other seats

Republican efforts – and money – have largely shifted toward other parts of the state, like the 21st Senate District running from Racine through Franklin and Greendale, and the 17th District covering the southwestern corner of the state.

Roberts' campaign finance reports show about $144,000 worth of in-kind contributions from CERS, and no additional monetary contributions. The committee has not directed any money to Roberts in the month of October.

Republican candidate Jim Croft, running in the 21st District, lists from CERS about $602,000 of in-kind contributions and another $1.9 million in monetary support. Republican Sen. Howard Marklein, defending his 17th District seat, lists about $769,0000 of in-kind contributions from CERS and another $1.2 million in monetary support. Both received party investments in October.

Roberts himself has raised a total of $284,147.

Democratic money has also been concentrated elsewhere. Vining has raised $344,556 this year. She lists about $111,000 of in-kind contributions from the State Senate Democratic Committee and no additional monetary support from the committee.

In contrast, the SDDC has given Democratic candidate Trevor Jung more than $2 million in monetary contributions for his 21st District race and $119,000 of in-kind support, and nearly $1.5 million in monetary contributions and $92,818 of in-kind support to state Rep. Jenna Jacobson in her effort to unseat Marklein in the 17th District.

Neither campaign is engaging meaningfully in the advertising wars dominating so many races across the state, either.

Affordability tops both candidates' priorities

For both Vining and Roberts – and in line with statewide polling – the cost of living is the prevailing concern they hear from voters in the district.

"I just look at all the opportunities that I was blessed to have growing up here in this district," Roberts said. "I see those opportunities being threatened for now, not just my children, but that next generation that's going to inherit the state."

Vining also said she's never heard so much from voters about utility costs.

"I would say over the last two months, it has shifted from being people concerned about affordability, as we've been hearing since June, to really, people being afraid that they're not going to be able to afford to survive," Vining said, adding that the concern especially permeates among older voters on fixed incomes.

Elected officials need to offer a "swift and comprehensive response" to those concerns, Vining said. While some things, like gas prices, are largely dictated by national policies, Vining said lawmakers need to boost general school aids and adjust shared revenue for local governments to manage property tax increases. Lawmakers should also quickly enact new regulations on data centers, she said, to ensure energy costs aren't shifted onto ratepayers.

For Roberts, the solution is enacting policies "to make sure that we are getting more of everyone's hard-earned money back in their pockets."

He pointed to the collapse in the state Senate this spring of a popular bipartisan tax deal offering school funding and individual tax relief from the state's projected surplus, now estimated to be near $3 billion, and noted Vining joined many Democrats in voting against the deal in the Assembly.

Vining and other Democrats who opposed the bill cited the need to keep the surplus in place in case the state's economy experiences a downturn.

Vining sees opportunities for new priorities with a Democratic majority

After seven years in the Assembly, Vining sees a few new opportunities in the Senate: for one, contributing to a Democratic majority if they pick up the two seats needed to secure it. Vining said she would like to chair a legislative committee and hold hearings on bills that haven't received them under Republican leadership, including offering a BadgerCare public option.

The Democratic lawmaker said she would also hold quarterly meetings with the lawmakers representing the Assembly districts within the 5th, "getting to know our district together and building relationships and figuring out where we have common ground that serves the common good."

Asked about her accomplishments in office, Vining quickly pointed to bills signed into law by Gov. Tony Evers this year ills that extend postpartum Medicaid coverage for mothers and require insurance to cover additional cancer screenings for women with dense breast tissue.

Both had appeared fated to die in the Assembly but were dramatically revived after a public, vocal push by Democrats and a behind-the-scenes effort by a group of determined Republicans.

"I'm proud that we didn't take no for an answer, and that we fought with everything we had, and we won," Vining said.

She also touted Democratic efforts while in the minority to shift policy conversations toward their priorities in areas including childcare, special education and mental health funding.

"We have shifted from on so many topics from if we're going to fund them to how we're going to fund them," she said.

Roberts would push to ease administrative rules and regulations in Wisconsin

Roberts sees in the Senate an opportunity to reduce the number of administrative rules and regulations on the books in Wisconsin, pointing to "red tape reset" proposals that have passed the Legislature with GOP support to be vetoed by the governor.

"If we're going to attract businesses to come in [to Wisconsin], we have to create an environment in the state that's attractive to them," he said, urging Republicans and Democrats to work together to find 10% of administrative rules that could be rolled back.

Roberts argued the same approach – "reducing the amount of administrative waste" – in healthcare can lead to a beneficial balance of cost, quality and access for patients.

The 5th Senate District includes Assembly Districts 13, 14 and 15. Vining currently represents the 13th Assembly District that now has an open race, and Democrat Angelito Tenorio represents the 14th. Tenorio is seeking reelection. Republican Rep. Adam Neylon, who is seeking reelection this fall while running in the Dec. 15 special election for Waukesha County executive, represents the 15th.

Jessie Opoien can be reached at jessie.opoien@jrn.com.
news.author: Journal Sentinel

news.title: Gas Prices, Housing, Interest Rates: Inside the US Cost-of-Living Picture Ahead of the Midterms
news.text:
As voters weigh the economic records of both parties ahead of the midterms, cost-of-living concerns have emerged as a defining issue. Some point to the 40-year high inflation under President Joe Biden while others blame President Donald Trump’s tariff policies and the conflict in Iran.

Democrats fault Trump for high gas prices and other expenses, while voters compare the cost-of-living differences between blue and red states.

As both parties trade blame for rising costs, here is a look at where their economic track records actually stand.

Throughout his 2024 campaign, Trump routinely promised to bring down inflation and restore affordability, and before the war in Iran began in late February, headline consumer inflation in the United States had been inching closer to the Federal Reserve’s elusive 2 percent target.

However, the inflation outlook changed significantly once the conflict broke out and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy prices.

Now approaching its ninth month, the war has kept the annual inflation rate in the United States persistently above 3 percent.

While energy-driven price hikes mirror the challenges the previous administration faced, Biden contended with an even more severe inflation shock. Under his presidency, annual inflation peaked at a 40-year high of 9.1 percent in June 2022, becoming a major vulnerability for his economic record. The annual inflation rate was 1.4 percent when he took office in January 2021.

Critics, including Republicans in Congress, blamed his energy policies for the rise in prices across the board, from gas stations to grocery stores.

Soon after taking office in 2021, Biden signed several executive orders targeting the fossil fuel industry, including canceling the Keystone XL pipeline permit and pausing new oil and gas leases on federal lands.

In response, energy companies curbed investments and scaled back expansion plans. Supply constraints unsettled energy markets, driving oil and gas prices significantly higher throughout 2021 and 2022.

Some prominent economists, including former Democratic Treasury Secretary Larry Summers, also pointed to the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan as a driver of inflation during Biden’s presidency. The stimulus plan was intended to prevent a post-pandemic recession.

Under Biden, the national average gas price reached an all-time high of $5.02 in 2022. It was not until late 2025, during the second Trump administration, that the national average slipped below $3.

Gas prices later surged in 2026 as crude oil climbed toward $100 a barrel in response to the war in Iran. This pushed the national average to about $4.50 per gallon in May 2026, the highest level of the year so far. Since then, prices have moderated somewhat, with the national average standing at about $4.27 per gallon on Oct. 27.

When gas prices began to surge in 2021, Biden initially dismissed the inflation as “transitory.” He blamed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 for rising prices. As prices kept rising, he began accusing companies of price gouging.

The consumer price index (CPI) increased by an average of 5 percent per year during Biden’s presidency, compared to 1.9 percent annually during Trump’s first term. To date, average annual inflation under Trump’s second term has been nearly 3 percent.

Cumulatively, the CPI rose by more than 21 percent during Biden’s four-year term, compared to 7.7 percent during Trump’s first term. And since Trump began his second term, overall prices have risen by about 6 percent in total.

Although inflation slowed down toward the end of the Biden administration, the cumulative effect sapped workers’ wages. Real (inflation-adjusted) earnings declined for more than two years, which eroded the public’s purchasing power and applied financial pressures on families.

Despite headwinds ranging from the Iran war to expansive new tariffs, inflation under the Trump administration has run lower than during Biden’s presidency. Furthermore, underlying inflation has been tame: Stripping out volatile energy and food prices, the annual core inflation rate came in at 2.6 percent in September.

Yet almost two years into Trump’s presidency, Americans remain deeply frustrated by the cost of living, which continues to shape their views of the broader economy and their choices at the voting booth.

Heading into the midterms, various polls show that Trump’s approval ratings on the economy and inflation are firmly underwater. An Oct. 6 Economist–YouGov poll found that 36 percent of respondents approved of the president’s handling of the economy.

By comparison, Biden had polled better heading into the 2022 midterms. An Economist–YouGov survey from October of that year found that 40 percent approved of Biden’s handling of the economy.

The growing dissatisfaction is also reflected in consumer sentiment.

The University of Michigan’s Consumer Sentiment Index—a widely watched barometer of the public’s confidence in the current and future economic landscape—was 48 in October, the second-lowest reading in its nearly 75-year history. The lowest recording, 44.8, occurred in May of this year.

While sentiment continues to deteriorate, real median income has improved, and the poverty rate has steadily declined in the last few years.

Median weekly earnings of full-time wage and salary workers is up about 4 percent since the first quarter of 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

According to Deutsche Bank economists, there is a growing disconnect between how consumers feel about the economy and the actual economic statistics.

In a recent note emailed to The Epoch Times, they explained that “households might be responding to the cumulative price/cost of living shock since COVID rather than the spot inflation rate.”

They added that ongoing housing affordability challenges and growing worries about artificial intelligence (AI) are also weighing on consumer sentiment.

“The cost of everything from groceries and gas to housing and childcare is going up because of choices made by Donald Trump’s administration,” former Vice President Kamala Harris wrote in an Oct. 20 post on X.

Speaking at a Michigan rally on Oct. 24, former President Barack Obama similarly blamed Trump’s policies for rising costs, pointing to the war in Iran “that nobody asked for.”

Many consumers continue to cite the cost of energy—from gasoline to utility bills—as major concerns heading into the midterms, making affordability a prominent issue for policymakers and political candidates alike.

Regarding prices at the pump, a July report by the Institute for Energy Research (IER) found that in states in which Democrats controlled the governorship and the legislature, gasoline prices averaged $3.69 per gallon, compared with Republican states, where gasoline averaged $3.14 per gallon, a gap of $0.55 per gallon.

According to the report, much of this gap is due to higher gasoline taxes, hostility toward refineries, and other policies that drive up fuel costs.

These costs would likely be passed on to consumers in the form of price hikes.

Diesel prices have also rocketed during the Iran conflict. While the fuel cost is down from its record high of almost $6.53 in September, the average price per gallon is still firmly above $6, about 40 percent higher than a year ago.

Regarding electric bills, an IER and Always On Energy Research analysis found that blue-state residents pay, on average, 42 percent more for electricity than red-state residents.

The report attributes this difference to heavy-handed regulation, including net-zero emissions mandates, carbon pricing and cap-and-tax regimes, and other laws intended to replace fossil fuels with wind and solar energy, IER spokesman Alex Stevens told The Epoch Times.

Like electricity costs, housing affordability diverges between red and blue states.

According to a 2025 Realtor.com report, the most affordable states for housing are in the South and Midwest.

The report notes that states in the South and West are building the most homes, with seven states in these two regions accounting for more than half of new-home construction permits issued across the country in 2024.

Grading states for affordability, the report says, “States in the South and Midwest received all of the good grades given out (As and Bs) on the basis of affordability and homebuilding; states in the West and Northeast, with generally stricter zoning and land use regulations, received all of the bad grades (Ds and Fs).”

Both the Biden and Trump administrations proposed measures they claimed would improve housing affordability after the unprecedented surge in record home prices following the COVID-19 pandemic. This past summer, lawmakers also passed the most comprehensive housing bill in decades—the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

The legislation included dozens of provisions to boost supply, including streamlining environmental reviews, encouraging states and localities to reform zoning and land-use guidelines, supporting housing modernization, and restricting large institutional investors from buying single-family homes.

“We haven’t built enough homes in this country, so the more we can prioritize supply-side initiatives, ultimately, the more stable and more affordable housing will become,” Frank Cassidy, former Federal Housing Administration commissioner, told The Epoch Times.

Housing starts have not yet returned to pre-2020 levels, and have been trending lower since hitting a 2022 peak. Currently, industry experts say the United States is short 4 million to 5 million homes.

The median sales price of existing properties has steadily increased since falling below $400,000 at the start of the year. August’s median existing-home sales price was $417,500, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Conversely, the median sales price of new houses sold in September was $400,400, up from $398,700 in January, Census Bureau data show.

But the cheaper new homes have not eased the crunch in the larger existing-home market.

Compounding the shortage, higher mortgage rates are pushing up monthly payments even further. The median monthly mortgage payment is almost $2,800—at a 7.4 percent mortgage rate, up more than 8 percent from a year ago, according to Redfin. As a result, many families are priced out of today’s housing market, which may present challenges for the Trump administration.

Trump has said lower interest rates would be “rocket fuel” for the U.S. economy.

One way to achieve this, according to the president, is for the Federal Reserve to act.

“Because the U.S. economy is so strong, regardless of the Fed’s formula, we should have the lowest interest rates in the world,” Trump told reporters ahead of the Fed’s September policy meeting.

But the central bank, like many of its counterparts, has been heading in the other direction.

The Fed followed through on its first quarter-point rate hike since July 2023 in September, and policymakers and markets alike are penciling in at least one more rate hike to prevent second- and third-order inflation effects.

The Treasury bond market has been in the spotlight since the outbreak of war in the Middle East, with key yields climbing to multi-decade highs.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield—a key rate that influences a range of business, consumer, and government borrowing costs—recently closed at its highest level since 2002, trading above 5.3 percent. The 10-year yield has since cooled off, sliding back to around 5 percent.

When Trump began his second term, the 10-year was around 4.6 percent, and it fell to as low as 3.93 percent in October 2025.

Markets will now wait to see whether manufacturers pass higher costs on to consumers, said Jeff DerGurahian, loanDepot’s head economist.

“If those costs begin showing up in both headline and core inflation, mortgage rates could remain elevated,” DerGurahian told The Epoch Times. “But if businesses absorb more of the increases, that could ease inflation concerns and give rates some room to improve.”

Higher interest rates have filtered through the U.S. housing market.

Mortgage rates are at their highest levels in three years, with the average 30-year fixed rate at 7.28 percent in early October, according to Freddie Mac.

The 30-year mortgage rate, which typically tracks the 10-year bond yield, slipped below 6 percent in late February for the first time since 2022.

The longer mortgage rates remain elevated, the harder it will be for younger people—an important voting bloc for the president in 2024—to achieve the dream of homeownership.
news.summary: Democrats blame Trump’s tariffs and the Iran war, Republicans point to Biden-era inflation, and voters feel squeezed.
news.author: Andrew Moran,Emel Akan,Kevin Stocklin
