The report attributes this difference to heavy-handed regulation, including net-zero emissions mandates, carbon pricing and cap-and-tax regimes, and other laws intended to replace fossil fuels with wind and solar energy, IER spokesman Alex Stevens told The Epoch Times.

Like electricity costs, housing affordability diverges between red and blue states.

According to a 2025 Realtor.com report, the most affordable states for housing are in the South and Midwest.

The report notes that states in the South and West are building the most homes, with seven states in these two regions accounting for more than half of new-home construction permits issued across the country in 2024.

Grading states for affordability, the report says, “States in the South and Midwest received all of the good grades given out (As and Bs) on the basis of affordability and homebuilding; states in the West and Northeast, with generally stricter zoning and land use regulations, received all of the bad grades (Ds and Fs).”

Both the Biden and Trump administrations proposed measures they claimed would improve housing affordability after the unprecedented surge in record home prices following the COVID-19 pandemic. This past summer, lawmakers also passed the most comprehensive housing bill in decades—the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act.

The legislation included dozens of provisions to boost supply, including streamlining environmental reviews, encouraging states and localities to reform zoning and land-use guidelines, supporting housing modernization, and restricting large institutional investors from buying single-family homes.

“We haven’t built enough homes in this country, so the more we can prioritize supply-side initiatives, ultimately, the more stable and more affordable housing will become,” Frank Cassidy, former Federal Housing Administration commissioner, told The Epoch Times.

Housing starts have not yet returned to pre-2020 levels, and have been trending lower since hitting a 2022 peak. Currently, industry experts say the United States is short 4 million to 5 million homes.

The median sales price of existing properties has steadily increased since falling below $400,000 at the start of the year. August’s median existing-home sales price was $417,500, according to the National Association of Realtors.

Conversely, the median sales price of new houses sold in September was $400,400, up from $398,700 in January, Census Bureau data show.

But the cheaper new homes have not eased the crunch in the larger existing-home market.

Compounding the shortage, higher mortgage rates are pushing up monthly payments even further. The median monthly mortgage payment is almost $2,800—at a 7.4 percent mortgage rate, up more than 8 percent from a year ago, according to Redfin. As a result, many families are priced out of today’s housing market, which may present challenges for the Trump administration.

Trump has said lower interest rates would be “rocket fuel” for the U.S. economy.

One way to achieve this, according to the president, is for the Federal Reserve to act.

“Because the U.S. economy is so strong, regardless of the Fed’s formula, we should have the lowest interest rates in the world,” Trump told reporters ahead of the Fed’s September policy meeting.

But the central bank, like many of its counterparts, has been heading in the other direction.

The Fed followed through on its first quarter-point rate hike since July 2023 in September, and policymakers and markets alike are penciling in at least one more rate hike to prevent second- and third-order inflation effects.

The Treasury bond market has been in the spotlight since the outbreak of war in the Middle East, with key yields climbing to multi-decade highs.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield—a key rate that influences a range of business, consumer, and government borrowing costs—recently closed at its highest level since 2002, trading above 5.3 percent. The 10-year yield has since cooled off, sliding back to around 5 percent.

When Trump began his second term, the 10-year was around 4.6 percent, and it fell to as low as 3.93 percent in October 2025.

Markets will now wait to see whether manufacturers pass higher costs on to consumers, said Jeff DerGurahian, loanDepot’s head economist.

“If those costs begin showing up in both headline and core inflation, mortgage rates could remain elevated,” DerGurahian told The Epoch Times. “But if businesses absorb more of the increases, that could ease inflation concerns and give rates some room to improve.”

Higher interest rates have filtered through the U.S. housing market.

Mortgage rates are at their highest levels in three years, with the average 30-year fixed rate at 7.28 percent in early October, according to Freddie Mac.

The 30-year mortgage rate, which typically tracks the 10-year bond yield, slipped below 6 percent in late February for the first time since 2022.

The longer mortgage rates remain elevated, the harder it will be for younger people—an important voting bloc for the president in 2024—to achieve the dream of homeownership.
news.author: Andrew Moran,Emel Akan,Kevin Stocklin

news.title: Blue Kansas? Voters in Kansas Weigh In as Democrats Gain in Senate Polls
news.text:
KANSAS CITY, Kan.—Kansans have long been known for their strong pro-Republican voting tendencies in national politics, but there are signs that’s changing as Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist megachurch pastor, gains ground in the polls against incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall.

Kansas Republicans aren’t escaping the growing backlash in the polls.

Hamilton currently leads in an average of four recent polls, 46 percent to Marshall’s 45 percent, with President Donald Trump recently traveling to the state to campaign for the Republican.

Kansas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years.

“It’s been a long time that we’ve waited to flip,” Rachel Smith, a voter in Johnson County, Kansas, and lifelong Democrat, told The Epoch Times when asked about the polling.

None of the voters who spoke to The Epoch Times in Johnson County or nearby Shawnee County said they were backing Marshall this year.

The fight for the governor’s mansion looks more secure for Republicans but remains close, as state Senate President Ty Masterson, a Republican, faces off against state Sen. Cindy Holscher, a Democrat.

Masterson is in a stronger position than his Senate Republican counterpart, with polls showing he leads Holscher by around 5.7 percentage points on average.

Many of Hamilton’s backers in the state told The Epoch Times they are or used to be Republicans. Here’s what some critical swing voters said about Republicans’ position in the state.

Andrew Howell, Shawnee County election commissioner, told The Epoch Times that even though Kansas is still in early voting, county turnout is high.

Shawnee County—home to the Kansas state capital, Topeka—is one of a handful of key eastern counties in Kansas that have voted for Democrats in recent cycles.

Turnout here is critical to Democrats winning statewide. So far, Howell said, they’re seeing it.

“We’re seeing pretty good numbers of folks showing up to vote,” he said.

In his 2020 election, which Marshall won by about 11 percentage points, Shawnee County and Riley County—home to Manhattan, Kansas—backed the Democrat in the Senate and presidential races.

Howell told The Epoch Times that Democrats seemed to be coming out in stronger numbers than Republicans so far.

“Of course, we have no way of knowing how they’re voting,” he said.

Howell said that about 70 percent of voters show up to cast their ballot on the first Tuesday in November.

“So the real question is: Who’s going to show up on Election Day?”

For analysts, a key question is also where they show up.

Democrats’ most important target is Johnson County, the state’s most populous. The largely suburban county within the Kansas City metro area, just west of the Missouri border, accounts for about one-fifth of the state’s population.

In 2012, the historically Republican-voting county supported GOP nominee Mitt Romney by about 17 percentage points. But in 2020, it backed Democrat Joe Biden by about 8 points. In 2024, Vice President Kamala Harris won by about 8.5 points.

In 2024, Trump gained just one percentage point more support in Kansas than in 2020, despite a highly favorable national environment for Republicans in 2024.

Several voters in Johnson County who spoke to The Epoch Times said they were reluctant to vote for Democrats but condemned the national party’s direction under Trump.

Voters in the western parts of the state tend to favor Republicans more, and turnout here will be a top priority for the party.

The few blue eastern counties, because of their population and growing distance from Republicans, could be pivotal in the coming election.

Several Kansas voters spoke to The Epoch Times.

Debbie Severson of Johnson County said she opposes the two-party system entirely.

“I have to be Democrat,” the recently retired massage therapist said when asked which party she’s more aligned with.

“About six months to a year ago, I would have voted differently for Senate, but I’m not a fan of who we have right now,” she said, referring to Marshall. “I was questioning the other person that was running. … But he has proven to stand for what my beliefs are.”

Severson criticized Trump’s handling of the Iran war and international affairs.

“I think we continue to tear our relationships with other countries, and that’s hurting us in every direction,” she said.

Asked about the signs the state may be shifting toward Democrats, Severson said she thinks “people are finally realizing that you know you have to do your due diligence.”

Several Republicans said they were particularly unhappy with Trump.

Johnson County voter Deborah Brand is a registered Republican and former Republican committee chairperson, but has recently voted largely for Democrats since Trump’s election.

“Don’t like the man. I find him a sad representation of who we are,” Brand said.

She said she voted for Democrats in the gubernatorial and Senate elections this year because she felt the state “needs checks and balances we don’t have.”

The former chairperson said she had been moving away from Republicans since the Tea Party movement grew.

She hasn’t lost faith in the party entirely. Brand said she thinks that the state could swing back with a more moderate Republican.

“Kansas has always been very Republican. I think if there were a decent candidate, they would remain Republican. I have not changed my affiliation,” she added, saying this allows her to vote in the Republican primary.

Dennis, a voter from Overland Park who declined to share his last name, told The Epoch Times that he is a Republican but voted for Democrats in both the Senate and governor races.

“I’ve been voting Democratic ever since Trump was elected,” Dennis said. “I’m a Bob Dole, Dwight Eisenhower Republican, not a Trumper.”

Asked if he was aware of his state’s shift to the left, the part-time Republican said he believes it’s because of Trump’s policies.

Dennis said he believes Hamilton is a “man of principle.”

As for his governor pick, the voter said he is specifically concerned about needing more balance in state leadership.

“We need some Democratic representation in Topeka. And dominance by the Trump Republicans is bad for our state,” he said.

He accused Republicans of being too closely aligned with Trump at this point, calling for the president’s impeachment.
news.author: Joseph Lord

news.title: Democrats have a 2028 problem: Their candidates
news.text:
The Merriam-Webster definition of the word awkward is “having or showing a lack of grace, skill, or ease.” And given what we’ve witnessed from potential 2028 Democratic nominee Kamala Harris over the years, and especially in recent weeks ahead of the midterm elections on the campaign trail, the former vice president’s photo really should be next to “awkward” in the dictionary.

“Never let somebody else’s limited ability to see your capacity be a limitation on your ambition. That’s their limitation. That’s not our limitation. That’s their limitation!” she recently exclaimed at a rally in Mississippi to almost no applause from the attendance.

news.title: Elder Black Texans pass the baton to next generation to keep up fight at ballot box
news.text:
Pam Gaskin, 79, remembers a time in Galveston County when her father would be required to pay poll taxes in the ‘60s so he could vote, a payment that wasn’t demanded of many white men in the South. 

She witnessed the power of a united Black community at the polls, setting state history for representation and, more recently, the damage that can come when they don’t. 

But this year, she said she is witnessing what she’s hoped for for years: a younger generation ready to take the reins. 

“I cannot fight this fight much longer. I think it’s time,” said Gaskin, who is a co-founder of Houston Voting Initiative, a nonpartisan voter resource organization. 

On the other end of the generational divide, Erika Harrison, 40, an attorney and social media creator who goes by @blackgirlswhobrunch, has spent the past few months taking a break from posting food-related content and using her platform to mobilize her audience to vote. 

“I do believe there is a changing of the guard, but I also think we aren’t doing what they used to do,” she said. “There are so many generational differences.”

The nation’s eyes are on Texas, with major polls showing key down-ballot Democratic candidates in statewide races holding razor-thin leads against Republicans. For Democrats to win, they must have an extraordinary turnout by their base, coupled with a share of disaffected Republican and unaffiliated voters. That base, especially in Harris County and East Texas, has been Black voters.

Young Black voters, from high school to college to older millennials, have helped Harris County, home to the state’s largest Black population and one of the largest in the country, set records in the primaries and on the first day of early voting. 

Texas has more Black voters than any other state. As of 2022, Pew Research found that Texas had the largest population of Black eligible voters of any state: 2.9 million, or about 14% of all eligible voters. Black voters are a core part of the Democratic base, making up about one-fifth of Texas’ likely Democratic primary voters and 11% to 13% of the general electorate, according to previous reporting. 

Unlike older generations, which focused largely on equality and civic rights issues, this younger demographic focuses more on issues that affect their day-to-day lives — for example, affordability, the environment and job security. 

“There has been too much foolishness,” said Evan Robinson, a junior at Texas Southern University and vice president of the campus NAACP chapter, who is helping his fellow students vote this year. “For a long time there was a feeling that our voice doesn’t matter, but now we are waking up to the fact that if we don’t do something, it will only get worse. Politics affects you whether you like it or not.” 

Voting rights advocates believe this signals that the Black vote will once again determine the fate of state and national elections, but this time, a younger, more energized voter base is joining the effort, potentially recreating the momentum that had once made this demographic a voting powerhouse in the 70s and 80s.

“Every generation needs to determine what freedom means to them. We have to redefine what freedom means in this current climate,” said Annie Benifield, the other co-founder of Houston Voting Initiative. 

What is the Black vote and what happened to it?

The Black vote in Texas and across the nation has often been driven by people over 55 years of age, with younger generations often lagging behind since the end of former President Barack Obama’s term. However, voting analysts and advocates say a shift is beginning in Harris County and statewide, as a newer generation is getting involved, not only in voting but also in organizing.

Stephanie Williams, senior state organizing manager for Black Voters Matter, looked across the Texas Southern University campus in Houston earlier this month, relieved to see students asking questions about how to vote and where to go during the midterm elections.

“We’ve been working with students in Texas, especially here in Houston. We’ve registered over 60,000 young people to vote. That is the energy we’re creating, and now that we’ve got all these young people on the voting rolls, the next step is educating them on how to vote, where to vote, and creating a vote plan,” Williams said. “But also turning them into organizers, strategists, to really begin building that infrastructure that we’re envisioning.”

The younger generation is focused on issues like young educated Black women being laid off from federal government jobs due to the Department of Government Efficiency, or DOGE, cuts and the end of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion programs; economic downturn, Flock cameras, data centers, and lack of affordable housing. 

“When this country gets a cold, Black Americans get the flu. If there’s an increase in unemployment, you’ll see double that for Black Americans,” she said. “You have Gov. Greg Abbott appointing people to the boards of HBCU’s who we don’t believe will take these schools to the next level. There’s just so much.” 

Michael Adams, a political science professor at Texas Southern University and founding director of the Barbara Jordan Public Policy Research and Survey Center, said the Black vote in the state is concentrated in Houston, San Antonio, Dallas and some areas in East Texas. He said these areas are key for candidates hoping to win an election, which is why the Black vote has mattered so much for decades. 

The power of the Black vote and representation in Texas was most consistent between 1965 and 2012, after the Voting Rights Act passed, driven by enthusiasm among Black voters who knew the privilege of going to the polls. 

“My parents didn’t get to vote until their 50s when the Voting Rights Act was passed. I remember the marches; I marched in college back in Alabama to prevent a prison being built next to an HBCU,” said Benefield. “I have always known the importance of the vote.” 

National Black turnout peaked in 2008 and 2012 after a small dip in the early 2000s, with former President Barack Obama on the ballot. In 2012, Black turnout exceeded white turnout in several Southern states, a first in American history. 

Since Obama’s era, Democratic candidates have struggled to bring back the Black vote in Texas and nationwide, and voting analysts say it has been due to a generational shift and a lack of strategies to engage with a younger and fast-growing demographic of Millennials and Gen Z.

For example, former President Joe Biden won Harris County by 13 points in 2020. However, Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris won the county by only 5.5 percentage points in the 2024 election cycle.

“We stopped engaging and participating,” Benefield said. “We thought we had overcome, but we hadn’t.” 

Voting experts also cite a litany of challenges, including the end of party-line voting in 2020, consistent redistricting and a lack of young candidates, which have led to confusion and burnout among younger voters. 

“Sometimes as Black people we don’t craft or have a succession plan, and I think that is very important,” Adams said. 

However, younger Black voters seemingly returned in large numbers this year. 

During this year’s primary, Harris County Clerk Teneshia Hudspeth reported record turnout for a non-presidential primary, with more than 565,000 voters in 12 days. The Houston Defender reports that, based on demographic estimates, roughly 118,650 of those votes came from Black voters. 

“The message we found that has resonated with young people is not being candidate-specific but speaking about healthcare and then folding in candidates,” said Brianna Brown, executive director of the Texas Organizing Project. 

Williams credits this new enthusiasm to different strategies to engage younger voters, but also to a generational shift in which younger Black voters seem ready to take the reins from older organizers. 

“Black women will always do our thing, especially to save democracy, so you can count on that,” Williams said. “But we also understand the assignment too. It can’t just be us. We got to get our brothers. We got to bring our kids. We are still on the front lines doing the organizing, but this is inclusive of us, because at the end of the day, it’s about all of us.” 

A change in strategy 

Svante Myrick, president of the People For the American Way Foundation, stood outside The Breakfast Klub in Houston’s historic Black neighborhood of Midtown, where he told an audience gathered for a community event about the importance of voting in this year’s election. 

“The entire world hinges on what happens here in Houston and Texas,” he said, pointing to the murals his organization commissioned that encourage voting. 

The block party and mural unveiling, supported by Harris County officials, including County Commissioner Rodney Ellis, is one example of how voting organizations, advocates, and candidates are encouraging civic participation among a younger generation beyond voting stickers and campaign events. 

“Given the current state of the world, we got to do our part, whatever that might be,” said Preston Gaines, a 36-year-old architect, artist and founder of Inanimate Nature, who, along with other artists, helped paint the murals in Houston. 

Voting-participation organizations across the state are reaching younger Black voters by working with social media creators and influencers, creating voter guides, hosting community parties, and more, and younger generations are responding positively to these efforts. 

“We are seeing Gen-Zers across the world changing the way our future looks,” said Marshall Bradley, a 25-year-old architectural assistant at Inanimate Nature, who has been voting since 2020. “I think these recent events have shown us, ‘Oh, this is why voting is important,’ and living through these events has motivated us to vote.” 

Bradley said many Black people in his generation are particularly interested in this election because current decisions directly affect their future. 

“It has become almost irresponsible for us to not vote,” he said. “We have to vote to keep the rights our founding fathers established.” 

The shift to a younger demographic doesn’t mean the older generation is forgotten, said U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, D- Dallas, who stood outside a voting booth in Houston, where lines stretched around the block, but more of a need for multiple Black generations to come together at an important point in time.

“No matter where I meet some of our seniors, I know they were active,” she said. “The fight for the ballot box right now is there, but I think that the fight looks a little different. I think right now that we have to emphasize the things that our younger generation is most concerned about.” 

For many years, politicians catered to the Black vote by showing up at churches and telling congregations to vote, expecting the message to echo throughout the community. However, times have changed, and older advocates and organizers have struggled until recently to catch up.

“How the Democratic Party engages with Black voters, especially when Millennials become the largest voting bloc, is going to require a lot more work,” Harrison said. 

Candidates seem to have noticed this campaign cycle. For example, state Rep. James Talarico has appeared on popular national Black podcasts like The Breakfast Club, attended Sunday Funday in Houston and gave a commencement address at Paul Quinn College in Dallas. Gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa joined an interview discussion with Black Girls Politickin and campaigned in Houston’s historic Black community of Acres Homes, and state Rep. Vikki Goodwin appeared at Prairie View A&M’s homecoming.

“You see now that elected officials are going to these Black restaurants, Black bars, and sometimes feel like it’s performative, but where else are you gonna find your core audience,” Harrison said. 

The main difference between younger and older Black generations is that Millennials and Gen-Zers feel the need for candidates to court their vote, rather than going to the polls out of a sense of duty passed down from the Civil Rights movement. 

Some younger Black voters are focused on class issues over racial progress that dominated voting discussions in the past, while others are more focused on getting younger candidates instead of supporting those who look like them. 

This year, young Black voters’ enthusiasm seems driven more by desperation and anger than by genuine support for candidates, and if the Democratic Party wants to carry this forward to the presidential election, it must offer hope. 

“It’s not like the optimism you felt with Obama, or even the kind of excitement I felt when Kamala Harris was running. It feels like okay, we gotta go save this country again,” Harrison, a content creator, said. “It feels more out of duty and obligation and an understanding of what’s at stake.” 

It’s still unclear whether the Black vote will change the political landscape in Texas this year, but Crockett said that to see this year’s momentum continue into the 2028 presidential election, candidates must stop taking their community’s vote for granted. 

“I do think there will be conversations that the Democratic Party is going to have to have right now, because I think there is frustration that is taking place with Black communities, specifically with the Democratic Party, the lack of investments that are made into Black people when we know that Black people have held this party down,” she said.
news.summary: For Democrats to win in Texas, young Black voters must vote in record numbers. Harris County advocates are betting on it.
news.author: Stephen Simpson

news.title: Six charts that explain how Texas’ suburbs became a midterm battleground
news.text:
Texas’ booming suburbs have been a hard-fought political battleground for several cycles. How they vote in next week’s election could decide the state’s marquee races, including the U.S. Senate, and scores of critical legislative contests.

The suburbs of Texas have long occupied the middle ground between Democratic-dominated cities and dark-red rural areas where Republicans run up the score. But from Colleyville to Conroe to Cedar Park to Cibolo, that map is blurring, as once-rural areas become exurbs, exurbs become suburbs and inner-ring suburbs become economic powerhouses in their own right. Suburban counties are getting more populous and more diverse, and they make up a larger share of the electorate each cycle.

They’ve also been an anchor for Democrats, who’ve kept their numbers relatively stable in the suburbs since 2018 as the rest of Texas moved rightward. But that doesn’t mean the suburban counties behave uniformly, even within the same metropolitan areas.

In the Dallas-Fort Worth area, for example, Irving, a large inner-ring suburb west of Dallas, moved over 15 percentage points toward Republicans between 2020 to 2024, according to VoteHub — a much larger shift than the state as a whole. Plano, a suburb north of Dallas and farther from the city center, shifted only 6 points rightward, less than the state as a whole but still favoring Republicans. And Midlothian, a suburb south of Dallas on the outer ring, shifted nearly 9 points toward Democrats, while still voting solidly red overall.

Both U.S. Senate candidates first won elected office representing suburban state legislative seats — Ken Paxton, the Republican, in McKinney in 2002, and James Talarico, the Democrat, in Round Rock in 2018.

To flip Texas, Talarico and other Democrats will need to do more than just match their party’s prior high-water marks in these counties — they’ll need to post historic numbers in the suburbs, taking advantage of their growth and President Donald Trump’s poor approval rating. To keep the state under Republican control, Paxton and other members of his party must, as they did in 2024, hold the suburbs steady — or at least limit the anticipated leftward shift from spiraling out of control. 

Hanging in the balance are competitive races down the suburban ballots across Texas, from the state Legislature to counties’ governing commissioners courts.

The Texas Tribune defined 16 counties as “suburban,” starting with the counties designated as “large fringe metros” — located in, but not central to, metro areas of 1 million or more people — in the National Center for Health Statistics’ 2023 urban-rural classification scheme. We then filtered out any counties with populations under 50,000, as well as ones that surpassed the 50,000 threshold but did not contain at least one city, or part of a city, with a population of 25,000 or more. The aim was to capture only counties with some degree of the density associated with suburbs, weeding out the more remote or sparsely populated exurbs and rural areas. 

This method means we aren’t accounting for the suburban parts of “urban counties,” such as the outlying communities of Harris and Dallas counties beyond the cities of Houston and Dallas. Take it as an analysis of the suburban counties, but one that does not grab every suburban resident.

We made one exception to the methodology, choosing to include Collin County even though it was classified as a “large central metro” — the NCHS’ label for the most populous urban counties. We included it among the suburbs due to its proximity to Dallas and Fort Worth and its widely recognized status as a suburban county in the larger metropolitan area.

The resulting 16 suburban counties vary by population, from Collin County’s nearly 1.2 million people to Rockwall and Hunt Counties, which have between 120,000 and 145,000. And their partisanship differs across the board. Fort Bend and Hays counties, for example, have narrowly preferred Democrats in recent cycles; some of the less populous suburban counties, like Parker and Comal, are deeply Republican. And Montgomery County, the sprawling home of places like Conroe and The Woodlands, provided the largest margin, by raw votes, to President Donald Trump of any U.S. county in 2024.

But some patterns are evident across the state’s suburbs. Below, we illustrate some of them, along with a zoomed-in look at what is happening in the Dallas-Fort Worth area — the epicenter of Texas’ relentless suburban sprawl.

The suburbs are growing every election

Each election, Texas’ suburban counties are becoming a larger portion of the electoral pie.

In just eight years, the 16 counties we’ve classified as suburban grew from about one-fifth to nearly one-quarter of the state’s registered voter population, inching up each election cycle. 

That growth is especially evident in the counties that contain more outer-ring suburban communities, and in the exurbs of the metro areas that comprise the Texas Triangle — Dallas-Fort Worth, Houston, San Antonio and Austin. Much of the population increase is fueled by people moving from elsewhere in Texas and from out of state.

Each of the suburban counties we’ve identified increased its number of registered voters by at least 30% since 2012. In Comal County, which is between San Antonio and Austin, registered voters increased by 83% from 2012 to 2024, the biggest jump among these counties. 

The increasing diversity of Texas’ suburbs

It’s not just white soccer moms in the suburbs anymore.

Suburban counties are diversifying almost twice as fast as the rest of Texas. In 2014, people of color made up 40% of the population in the 16 counties. By 2024, they made up nearly half the suburban populace.

That diversification is reshaping some of the communities that will determine the 2026 election. 

In Collin and Fort Bend counties, both of which are between 22% and 24% Asian, the voting patterns of the Indian American and Vietnamese American communities will especially shape local races. Nationally, Democrats tend to do better with Indian Americans while Vietnamese Americans tend to lean more Republican.

But in Texas, Republicans have made significant gains with Indian Americans and with Asian voters broadly, helping to stymie the leftward shift of counties like Collin and Fort Bend in 2024. 

Democrats are hopeful they can do better with Asian Americans this cycle amid the economic frustration extending to virtually all corners of the electorate, as well as an increasingly viral wave of anti-Indian hate from GOP activists particularly in the Dallas-area suburbs.

These counties are also expanding as they grow more diverse. Some of the most pronounced examples are Hays and Williamson counties, which have both grown by over 23% between 2020 and 2025. That puts both Austin-area counties among the fastest-growing in Texas. Over that same period of time, the white share of the population dipped below 50%.

The blue shift of the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs

When Ted Cruz ran for Senate in 2012, he ran up the score in the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs.

Take the six major counties in the metro area — Dallas, Tarrant, Collin, Denton, Rockwall and Wise, each divided in the maps above by their current state House districts. In 2012, Collin and Denton counties were an abundance of safely red seats, as were the Tarrant County districts outside Fort Worth’s blue core. 

Note: Past election results are projected to the current Texas House boundaries, which were enacted in 2023.
Source: Texas Legislative Council
Credit: Apurva Mahajan

Six years later, the map looked very different. Cruz’s margin in Collin and Denton counties narrowed, and O’Rourke even won a district anchored in Plano. Territory in northwestern Dallas County — which includes suburbs like Addison and Farmers Branch — went from red to blue. And Tarrant County experienced major shifts.

In all, Democrats, riding on Senate candidate Beto O’Rourke’s coattails, flipped six state house seats in the region that year, all of which included pieces of the suburbs.

In 2024, Cruz ran more than 5 percentage points ahead of his 2018 campaign. But that shift came from other places. Collin and Denton counties stayed a similar shade of light red, while Texas as a whole moved right.

The suburbs are still Republican — but less so than they used to be

The coalition Texas Republicans built in the 20th century that came to dominate the state has always relied heavily on middle-class and upper-middle-class suburbanites.

Once many of the suburban counties turned red, they never looked back. Montgomery County, for example, has voted red in every U.S. Senate race in Texas since 1988.

But in recent years, some have broken the trend. Fort Bend County, southwest of Houston, voted for a Democratic Senate candidate in 2018 for the first time in 30 years — a pattern it has repeated in every Senate contest since. 

Taken together, the suburban counties have stayed red. But the margin has shifted enormously. Cruz won the suburban counties by 33 percentage points in 2012. Just six years later, his margin had fallen to 15 points — a smaller victory that nevertheless proved critical, given that he narrowly lost the combined vote across Texas’ other 238 counties.

Party operatives attribute the change to a combination of growth — including millions of new people arriving from out of state — and, in some areas, frustration among longer-term suburban Republicans as the GOP has shifted from the Bush country club model to the party of Trump and MAGA.

“I think you are seeing people who were part of a Republican Party that saw itself as representing upwardly mobile, younger voters,” said Wayne Thorburn, who served as executive director of the Republican Party of Texas from 1977 to 1983. “These are all the people that Trump has lost.”

Barry Jacobs, a 62-year old attorney in Waxahachie, is one such voter. Prior to 2016, he had voted Republican in every election he had ever participated in. But he became dismayed by what he sees as the embrace of corruption among some members of the Republican Party and the push toward culture wars.

In 2018, he voted for Cruz. But in 2024, Jacobs voted for Democrat Colin Allred. And he says he’s voting for Talarico this year. 

He suspects there are other center-right voters like him in Ellis County, south of Dallas, who are being turned off by the party. Culture war attacks — like claiming teachers are transitioning kids in elementary school — may be less effective in tight-knit communities in the outer suburbs.

“We have one high school,” Jacobs said. “Everybody in town went to that high school…[teachers] live in the community. Everybody knows them. It’s not like this is a bunch of blue-haired hippies from California who are coming to brainwash our kids. [They’re] our neighbors. They go to church with us.”

In Texas’ suburbs, more growth tends to mean a bluer electorate

Every county we defined as suburban grew at a faster rate than the overall state between 2012 and 2024. Twelve of the 16 counties also shifted toward Democrats by a bigger margin than the state did as a whole, using the metric of Cruz’s initial Senate victory and his most recent one.

The trendline also demonstrates that the more a suburban county grew over that 12-year period, the more it shifted toward Democrats.

Most of these counties voted for Cruz in both elections. But their margin changed. In Galveston County, which had the lowest growth rate of the bunch, at 21%, the leftward shift was marginal. Allred only performed 1.3 percentage points better than Cruz’s 2012 opponent, Paul Sadler.

Kaufman County, meanwhile, nearly doubled in population, growing at the fastest rate of all the suburban counties. It shifted 20 percentage points toward Democrats between 2012 and 2024.

The biggest political shifts also belong to the two most populous suburban counties — Collin and Denton — which moved 26 and 24 percentage points toward Democrats, respectively.

The trend also extends to presidential elections. Between 2016 and 2024, Texas lurched to the right, with Trump improving on his prior margin. But in 14 of the 16 suburban counties, Kamala Harris outperformed Hillary Clinton.

Where are new D-FW suburbanites coming from?

Much of the changing face of the Dallas-Fort Worth suburbs owes to migration from other places in the United States — and in particular, California.

Six of the top ten out-of-state counties where people are moving from are in California. The other four include some of the largest cities in America — Phoenix, Chicago, Seattle and Las Vegas, respectively.

“Don’t California my Texas” has long been a rallying cry on the right. But there’s active debate over whether the Californians are importing the state’s liberal political philosophy, explicitly choosing Texas because of its differences, including its lower cost of living, or just relocating for work.

Exit polling can be an inexact science, but their findings suggest Republicans should not be so quick to diss California, or non-native Texans more broadly. 

In 2018, CNN found O’Rourke narrowly won native Texans, while Cruz dominated with people who have moved to the state. In 2024, the trend was nearly identical; Allred won people born in Texas by four percentage points, while Cruz won transplants by 16 percentage points.

“What I see is people coming from other states want it to stay the way it is,” said Jill Tate, the president of Texas Federation of Republican Women. “Some of the long-timers are like, I’m just ready for a change.”
news.summary: The state’s fast-growing suburban counties have gotten bigger, more diverse and bluer over time.
news.author: Apurva Mahajan

news.title: David Crowley rushes to shore up support with Black voters in Wisconsin governor’s race
news.text: MILWAUKEE — As former Vice President Kamala Harris entered a packed hotel downtown ballroom here Monday night to campaign for Democratic gubernatorial nominee David Crowley, the room erupted in a loud roar. She was repeatedly interrupted as she tried to speak by screaming and cheering attendees yelling, “I love you.”
news.author: Adam Edelman

news.title: The most vulnerable senators of 2026 less than a week before Election Day
news.text:
When CQ Roll Call first published this list for the 2026 election cycle a year and a half ago, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff was ranked the most vulnerable incumbent senator.

Things have changed. Just under a week out from Election Day, Ossoff now sits at the tail end of the rankings. Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales rates his reelection race as Lean Democratic, and major outside groups from both parties have pulled their ad spending from the state in recent weeks.

Ossoff’s drop is among a few changes we’ve made as we revisit this list for the final time before the midterm elections. The Senate battleground has remained relatively stable since the end of last month, with control of the chamber on the line. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win the majority — a prospect that looked highly unlikely for much of the cycle. 

The top four most vulnerable incumbent senators — Jon Husted of Ohio, Susan Collins of Maine, Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Roger Marshall of Kansas — are the same as our list from a month ago. While Husted, Collins and Sullivan have been in competitive races all year, Democrats continue to see deep-red Kansas as a pickup opportunity, and Inside Elections shifted the race rating in Democrats’ direction earlier this month. 

Other incumbents on this list, such as South Carolina’s Darline Graham and new entrant Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, face tougher-than-expected paths to reelection but remain favored to hold their seats. Still, their inclusion illustrates the tough environment Republicans find themselves in as they defend seats in deep-red territory that weren’t expected to be part of the battleground two years ago.

Nebraska’s Pete Ricketts remains on the list but falls a spot to No. 7 as the Republican appears to be in a stronger position to defeat independent Dan Osborn.

Races for a half-dozen open seats, which are not included on this list of vulnerable incumbents, will also be crucial to determining Senate control. Republicans have pickup opportunities in Michigan, Minnesota and New Hampshire, while Democrats are seeking to flip seats in Iowa, North Carolina and Texas. 

CQ Roll Call compiled these rankings based on interviews with party insiders, analyses of polls, campaign finances and independent expenditures, race ratings by political handicappers and candidates’ past performances.

The Ohio Senate race has become a big money brawl between Husted, who was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance’s remaining term, and Democrat Sherrod Brown, who served three Senate terms before losing to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. Brown raised a staggering $68.4 million through mid-October to Husted’s $19.9 million. Outside groups are investing heavily in the race, with crypto-related super PACs opposed to Brown among the top spenders. The outcome of the Senate race, as well as the gubernatorial contest, could signal whether Ohio will shift back to swing-state status for 2028.

Collins’ race against former state Senate President Troy Jackson remains tight, as she once again seeks to defy Maine’s Democratic tilt and win a record sixth term. The pair recently met for a series of heated debates, in which Collins touted her independence and track record of bringing federal dollars back home, while Jackson sought to tie her to President Donald Trump and underscore that Maine could influence which party controls the Senate. In a final ad released Tuesday, Jackson said he owes “nothing to the billionaires or Trump,” while a spot from Collins and the National Republican Senatorial Committee late last week highlighted Jackson saying, “Oh, shut up,” during a debate. 

Sullivan faces the same challenges other GOP candidates are confronting this year. But he’s also up against a high-profile Democratic challenger, another rival sharing his name and Alaska’s ranked choice voting system. There will be four candidates on the November ballot: Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent; Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola; retired teacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., listed with no party affiliation; and Republican Gerald Heikes, a perennial hopeful. Last week, the Justice Department took the unusual step of filing a lawsuit arguing that the “other” Dan Sullivan’s presence on the ballot would justify a delay in certifying the race if the incumbent loses.

Kansas hasn’t elected a Democratic senator since 1932, but Marshall is under pressure on multiple fronts as he seeks to turn back Democrat Adam Hamilton. The war in Iran and Trump’s tariffs are pushing up the cost of diesel fuel and fertilizer in this farming state. Marshall, a physician, also came under fire after The New York Times reported that his medical practice sued hundreds of patients for nonpayment of debts. Marshall and his supporters have cast Hamilton, pastor of the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation, as too liberal for the state, though the Democrat boasts endorsements from Republican former Govs. Mike Hayden and Bill Graves. 

Graham, who was appointed over the summer to fill the remaining term of her late brother, Lindsey Graham, is locked in an unexpectedly close race with Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews. South Carolina remains a deep-red state, and the incumbent has Trump’s backing as she seeks a full six-year term. But a political climate unfavorable to the GOP, combined with Graham’s lack of name recognition and political experience, are factors that have landed her on our list. Republican Rep. Ralph Norman, who lost a bitter primary runoff to Graham, told Fox News on Tuesday that Trump was trying to “force a candidate” on South Carolina voters. 

Hyde-Smith makes a late cycle debut on the list as her challenge from local district attorney Scott Colom heats up, though the limited polling of the race shows the incumbent ahead. The top Senate super PACs of both parties have recently gone up on air, while Trump and Kamala Harris have both visited the state in the past week. Democrats haven’t won a Senate race in Mississippi since 1982. To score an upset, Colom would need high turnout from Black voters, who Democrats believe are energized after the Supreme Court ruling weakening the Voting Rights Act, and also win over a certain chunk of Republican voters. 

After narrowly losing to Republican Deb Fischer two years ago, independent Dan Osborn is now challenging Ricketts, a former two-term governor and one of the wealthiest members of Congress. Osborn, a former union leader, has leaned into economic populism, casting Ricketts as an out-of-touch nepo baby. After Republicans circulated leaked audio of Osborn disparaging rural Trump voters, the independent candidate apologized. Despite Ricketts’ personal wealth, he’s getting an outside boost from the crypto-related Defend American Jobs super PAC. While there’s no Democrat on the ballot, Osborn could be hurt by the presence of three third-party candidates, though one has since dropped out and endorsed him.

Since topping our initial list of the most vulnerable senators, Ossoff has seen nearly everything go right for him. He raised an eye-popping $136.6 million through Oct. 14, swamping his Republican rival, Rep. Mike Collins, who brought in $10.7 million. Polls show him consistently in the lead. Collins has been dogged by a House Ethics inquiry and reports that his son-in-law shared antisemitic and white nationalist social media posts. At this point, the GOP’s main hope is that Ossoff somehow gets less than 50 percent, forcing him into a Dec. 1 runoff that could draw big spending if Senate control is on the line. 

Ryan Kelly contributed to this report.
news.author: Posted October 28, 2026 At 5:00am

news.title: New teachers union president wants to steer educators away from partisan politics
news.text:
The public education landscape is a bit of a minefield these days.

Inflation is blowing up school budgets. A new education tax credit that will direct federal tax dollars into private schools goes into effect in January. At the same time, the Trump administration is dismantling the Department of Education brick by brick.

Enter Princess Moss, the new face of the nation's largest labor union, the National Education Association. Its membership includes 3 million teachers and public workers from every state.

"Public education is under attack," she says. "Our students are under attack. The very foundation of this democracy is public education — that is under attack."

Her vision for the NEA — what she calls "resistance to renaissance" — has some markings of past leadership. It puts things like professional autonomy and community organizing front and center, but there is one stark departure she wants for the union.

"I want us to become our own political authority," Moss says. "Meaning that we're not aligning ourselves with a political party."

"I know this can work because I've done it before"

Princess Moss grew up the daughter of two school bus drivers in Spotsylvania County in rural Virginia. She recalls many teachers from her childhood who inspired her to pursue a career in schools. But her second grade teacher, Lucy T. Lewis, stands out. Moss remembers Lewis telling her she was smart back in 1968, even after she misspelled the word refrigerator in front of the entire class.

"I wanted to be just like Mrs. Lewis," she says. "Where you could help students learn and help students be the best that they could be even if they made a mistake every now and then."

Moss went on to work as an elementary school music teacher for more than 20 years in a neighboring county. Along the way she rose up the ranks in state union leadership, presiding over the Virginia Education Association from 2004 to 2008 and eventually moving up the ladder at the NEA. Moss now takes on the challenge of navigating a difficult political climate over her three-year term as president.

"We are the experts," she says. "We want to be at the decision-making tables."

One lesson she brings from her time in Virginia is that when she focused on the issues, there were allies to be found in unexpected places.

At the time, Virginia had a Democratic governor and Republican-controlled general assembly. She worked on building coalitions across the aisle and emphasized that public education is for everyone. With the midterms rapidly approaching, Moss said she's bringing that mentality to the NEA.

"Talk about your students"

"We're telling our members: 'Talk about your students. What do your students need?'" she says. "Don't make it a Democrat or Republican issue."

Michael Petrilli, the president of the right-leaning think tank the Fordham Institute, isn't quite so convinced: "Look, that would be a huge departure for the NEA," he says. "They have been stalwart supporters of the Democratic Party and vice versa."

In 2020, the NEA recommended Joe Biden for the office and in 2024 issued a formal endorsement for Vice President Kamala Harris.

Petrilli has long held reservations about the nation's teachers unions, saying their positions often block meaningful changes to teaching and perpetuate strict salary rules that can make it hard to recruit and fill certain jobs. But he says he's open to seeing where things go this year, especially with many state-level races leaning in the direction of the union's longtime allies — Democrats.

"This is going to put the unions in a very good position to be able to drive education policy," he says. "I think this is the question: What are they going to do with that power? What are they going to push these Democratic governors to get done?"

Even with Democrats favored to win some races and continued criticism of the union from some Republicans, Moss says she's focused on building a broad coalition of support for public schools.

"The bottom line is that we will work with those who want to put public education first," she says. "No matter what the political party, no matter what your inclination."

Edited by Nirvi ShahAudio story produced by Lauren Migaki
news.summary: NEA President Princess Moss wants to move her organization, the nation's largest labor union, toward issue-based advocacy — and away from party politics.
news.author: Sequoia Carrillo

news.title: US midterms 2026: What is the Samosa Caucus? And is it at risk of shrinking?
news.text:
The “Samosa Caucus,” the informal name for Indian-American members of the United States House of Representatives, has six members today, all of them Democrats.
After November 3, it will have at least four and at most six.
The math is simple, even if the politics are not.
Two members, Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois and Shri Thanedar of Michigan, lost Democratic primaries this year and will leave the House in January.
The four others, Ami Bera, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal and Suhas Subramanyam, are on the ballot in districts that favour their party.
Whether the group returns to its record strength of six, slips to five, or falls to four depends largely on two Democratic challengers: Amish Shah in Arizona’s 1st District and Pia Dandiya in Florida’s 22nd.
What is the Samosa Caucus?
The Samosa Caucus is a nickname, not an institution. It is a media-friendly label for lawmakers of Indian origin serving in the US Congress, and it is not an official caucus with a unified legislative programme.
The members share ancestry and, at present, a party, but they do not vote as a bloc and their policy emphases differ.
In practice, the label works as shorthand for a social and political network. Its members compare notes on Washington life, co-sign letters on issues that matter to the Indian-American community, and appear together at community events.
They have collaborated on matters such as high-skilled immigration, the US-India relationship and protection of religious places of worship from hate crimes.
The group has been entirely Democratic throughout its existence, although Indian-American Republicans are now contesting congressional seats in 2026, a point that complicates the idea of a single community voice.
How did the Samosa Caucus originate?
The story begins with the 2016 election. That November, four Indian Americans won seats in the House for the term that began in January 2017: Ami Bera of California, Ro Khanna of California, Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois and Pramila Jayapal of Washington state.
Bera was already a veteran, having first been elected in 2012. Khanna, Krishnamoorthi and Jayapal were newcomers. Kamala Harris, elected to the Senate the same year, made it five Indian Americans in the 115th Congress.
The nickname is widely credited to Krishnamoorthi. Reports from 2017 quote him using the phrase when he said that he, Jayapal, Bera, Khanna and everyone else were “at your service.”
Jayapal, for her part, told the same newspaper that the group could be called the Samosa Caucus or the “Fabulous Five,” whatever people wanted.
In January 2025, after taking the oath for the 119th Congress, Krishnamoorthi himself said that “eight years ago” he was proud to coin the phrase.
From the beginning, the group bonded quickly. Bera took on the role of mentor to the newcomers, advising them on settling into Washington, and was dubbed the “dean” of the group by an analyst.
One early collective action was a letter, started by Krishnamoorthi, urging the administration to address hate crimes after a spate of incidents. Over 70 other lawmakers signed it after the Indian-American members did.
Why “samosa”?
The name is a playful nod to the samosa, the fried, spiced, triangular snack that is among the most recognisable foods of the Indian subcontinent.
The term deliberately borrows the serious language of Washington, where “caucus” is the standard word for a group of lawmakers who organise around a shared identity or interest, and pairs it with something humble and universally loved.
Other labels were also available, including ones that referred to the group’s economic clout, but “Samosa Caucus” had a nicer ring to it and was original. That choice also helped the group present itself with humour rather than formality, which helped the phrase travel far beyond Capitol Hill.
The nickname has since entered the Indian political vocabulary in other ways. In June 2023, Prime Minister Narendra Modi referred to the Samosa Caucus in his address to a joint meeting of the US Congress, saying he hoped it would grow and bring the full diversity of Indian cuisine to the chamber.
Weren't there elected Indian Americans in Congress before?
The Samosa Caucus does stand on a much older foundation. Dalip Singh Saund, a Democrat from California, became the first Indian American in the House and served from 1957 to 1963.
Bobby Jindal, a Republican from Louisiana, was elected in 2004, making him the next to serve.
Bera’s 2012 win was the first time in decades that an Indian American won a House seat, and he reportedly said then that he hoped to see ten Indian Americans in the House someday.
The group grew gradually. Jayapal became the first Indian-American woman elected to the House in 2016.
Thanedar, a Michigan businessman, joined in 2023 after winning the 13th District, making the group five in the House.
In the 2024 elections, Subramanyam won Virginia’s 10th District, and the caucus reached six members when the 119th Congress opened in January 2025.
Krishnamoorthi said at the time that he was thrilled to see the group grow.
Who are the six current members?
Ami Bera represents California and has served since 2013. A physician by training, he is the longest-serving member of the group. His district is now numbered California’s 3rd and he is seeking re-election.
Ro Khanna represents California’s 17th District in the heart of Silicon Valley. First elected in 2016, he has built a national profile on technology policy, manufacturing, economic inequality and campaign-finance reform.
Khanna faces Republican Ritesh Tandon in California’s 17th, a rare race in which both candidates are of Indian origin. The district’s partisan lean gives Khanna a clear advantage.
Pramila Jayapal represents Washington’s 7th District, which covers Seattle. Born in Chennai, she moved to the United States at 16 and has represented the district since 2017. She is known for progressive positions on healthcare, immigration and workers’ rights.
Jayapal also faces an Indian-American Republican challenger, Nirav Sheth, in the strongly Democratic Seattle-area 7th District. She is the clear favourite on the basis of the district’s makeup.
Raja Krishnamoorthi represents Illinois’s 8th District. He ran for the Senate in 2026 rather than seek another House term.
Shri Thanedar represents Michigan’s 13th District and was seeking another term.
Suhas Subramanyam represents Virginia’s 10th District, in Northern Virginia, and entered the House in 2025 after serving in the Virginia General Assembly and working in the Obama administration.
Subramanyam is seeking a second term against Republican Dave Beckwith, a US Air Force veteran, in a Northern Virginia district with a Democratic-leaning electorate. Concerns about the economy, federal employment and public services are expected to shape the race.
Another Republican of Indian origin, Mahesh Ganorkar, is challenging Democratic Representative Valerie Foushee in North Carolina’s 4th District, which is considered safely Democratic.
The caucus cannot grow beyond six in January, because no other Indian American is a competitive House nominee this year. The Republican Indian-American candidates are challenging entrenched Democratic incumbents in districts where the odds are against them.
Why is the caucus at the risk of shrinking?
Both departures are the result of primary defeats, and each has a different story.
Krishnamoorthi gave up his House seat to run for the Senate in Illinois. In the Democratic primary on March 17, he lost to Illinois Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton, who took 40.39 per cent of the vote to his 32.71 per cent.
Had he won in November, he would have been only the second Indian American elected to the Senate, after Harris.
Thanedar sought re-election in Michigan’s 13th District and lost the August 4 Democratic primary to state Representative Donavan McKinney. McKinney won 51.9 per cent to Thanedar’s 48.1 per cent, ending the incumbent’s time in Congress.
The lesson is that Indian-American ancestry offers no automatic protection in primary contests.
Candidates still have to maintain party support, respond to local concerns and fend off challengers who can mobilise voters around generational change, ideology or dissatisfaction with incumbents.
Will Amish Shah win in Arizona’s 1st?
The most closely watched contest for the group is in Arizona. Amish Shah, an emergency-room physician and former state legislator, is the Democratic nominee in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, which covers Scottsdale, Fountain Hills, Cave Creek and parts of Phoenix.
Shah ran there in 2024 and lost to Republican David Schweikert by 3.8 points. Schweikert gave up the seat in 2026 to run for governor and was unsuccessful, so the seat is open.
Shah won this year’s Democratic primary on July 21, beating former broadcast journalist Marlene Galán-Woods. The result was widely reported as a setback for the national party’s House campaign arm, which had backed her.
He received about 39.5 per cent of the vote to her 34.3 per cent.
His opponent is Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker and broadcaster who has never held elected office. Feely originally ran in Arizona’s 5th District but switched to the 1st after US President Donald Trump, who had backed another candidate in the 5th, encouraged him to move.
Trump endorsed Feely in the primary and carried the district by about three points in 2024.
Both campaigns are fighting over labels. Feely and Republican groups cast Shah as a “socialist,” and Feely told the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in September that Democratic socialists “are the Democratic Party.”
Shah’s campaign called those allegations demonstrably false and points to a bipartisan legislative record and multiple police endorsements. He has said he is open to options other than single-payer healthcare.
Forecasters have been split. The Cook Political Report has rated the race Lean Democratic and Inside Elections rated it Tilt Democratic, though Cook had earlier called it a toss-up.
Public polling has been sparse and has shown a close race. Local analysts say turnout among independents may decide it.
If Shah wins, the caucus gets a replacement for one of the departing members. He would also be among the few Indian-American House members to represent a district that Republicans currently hold an edge in voter registration.
Will Pia Dandiya make it in Florida’s 22nd?
The second race is in Florida. Pia Dandiya, 39, a former teacher and high-school principal who later worked as a White House Fellow and at Apple, would be the first Indian American to represent Florida in Congress.
Born and raised in Palm Beach County to parents who immigrated from India, she is running on affordability, including housing, property insurance and healthcare costs, as well as public education and reducing corporate influence in Washington.
Her path was reshaped by the Florida redistricting that Governor Ron DeSantis and Republicans pursued mid-decade. Dandiya began the cycle challenging Republican Representative Brian Mast in Florida’s 21st District.
When the new map created an open 22nd District, which spans parts of Palm Beach, Broward, Collier and Hendry counties, she shifted to that race. She won the Democratic primary on August 18.
Her opponent is Casey Askar, a Marine Corps veteran and Naples businessman born in Iraq, who won a crowded Republican primary. Both Trump and DeSantis have endorsed him. Askar has also come under attack from Dandiya over healthcare and the Affordable Care Act.
The district was designed to favour Republicans, as part of a map that Florida Republicans hoped would flip four Democratic-held seats. The Cook Political Report rates the race Lean Republican with a partisan voting index of R+4, and Cook’s analysts wrote that Askar should have the edge while calling it a highly competitive race.
Polling suggests it is close. A Tavern Research survey showed a 50–50 tie, and a poll by Impact Research showed Dandiya ahead 46 per cent to 44 per cent. Outside groups are spending heavily, and Democrats added both Shah and Dandiya to their Red to Blue programme.
How are Indian-Americans in the US growing?
The Indian-American community is among the fastest-growing in the country. One recent estimate puts the diaspora at around 5.2 million people, making it the second-largest immigrant group in the United States.
Its members are concentrated in states and districts that can be decided by narrow margins, including Pennsylvania, Michigan, Georgia, Texas and New Jersey, as well as the suburbs of Atlanta and Washington.
A 2026 AAPI Data and AAPI Vote survey found that Asian Indian respondents favoured Democratic House candidates over Republican candidates by 66 per cent to 18 per cent.
That is a strong preference, but it does not mean every Indian-American voter is a Democrat, and national preferences will not necessarily decide individual district races.
Candidates from both parties are courting the community on the cost of housing and healthcare, jobs and the technology sector, legal immigration pathways, public safety and civil rights, and foreign policy including US-India ties.
With inputs from agencies
news.author: Anmol Singla

news.title: Mississippi turning? Democrats point to Republican ‘panic’ as Donald Trump flies in
news.text:
It’s 3pm so the staff in Borroum’s Drug Store are sweeping the floor and wiping the counters. Closing time here has been midafternoon since the 1920s but on this Monday, the town is deserted anyway. Everyone has gone out as far as the Crossroads Arena, on the east edge of the town, to wait for Donald Trump. Well, most people have.

“I’m not,” Lesley Lancaster says decisively when asked whether she will be going to the presidential rally.

“No. I don’t like crowds. I’m not waiting in line for nothing. I don’t have patience. But I think there’s a tonne of people out there. We are like five minutes from the Tennessee state line too. I was wondering why he chose Corinth out of all of Mississippi. But this was the crossroads for the civil war. Those train tracks I’m sure you crossed over: that was the front line.”

Lancaster is the latest in a line of Borroums and Mitchells who have operated the pharmacy here since AJ Borroum, a surgeon in the civil war, stopped off in Corinth while making his way back from Atlanta to Oxford in 1865. “A doctor buddy of his persuaded him to open a drugstore,” she says. Now, it has distinguished itself as the oldest drugstore in Mississippi and as a casually dazzling emporium of family artefact and authentic, unfussy Americana, with the pharmacy at the rear of the store, the original soda fountain with counter and swing stools as the centrepiece and, framed on the walls, weaponry and civil war paraphernalia passed from AJ Borroum through the generations. Family portraitures decorate the walls and, over the dining tables, an array of glass cases containing Native American arrowheads that another ancestor acquired in his youth.

“People who know about these things come in,” Lancaster says, “and they’ll say: ‘I know what case I would take.’ A lot of history here. But it’s just family stuff to us.”

Her father, Alexis, is the owner of Borroums now.

“But he goes by Lex,” she says, explaining, in an undiluted Mississippi accent, the thread of people named Alexis running through her family line.

“My brother’s name is Alexis and he goes by Lex. I named her Alexis,” she says, pointing to her daughter, who is helping in the store – “and she goes by Lex. And I have a Luke, too.”

The past is never dead: it’s a Mississippi phrase and a Mississippi truism. Corinth locals learned the president would be visiting with them just four days before the event itself. The fire service had to devise a lightning-fast management plan for traffic and people. The last president to speak in Corinth was Franklin Roosevelt, who addressed a crowd in November 1934 to praise the people of Alcorn country for embracing “an experiment that is going to succeed- the Alcorn Country Electric Power Association”.

Corinth is the biggest town in Alcorn county, which voted for Trump by 83 per cent, to 15 per cent for Kamala Harris in 2024. Trump won the state of Mississippi by a whopping 23 points. Although Republican alarm bells have been ringing for weeks in traditional strongholds of Iowa, Kansas and Ohio, where toss-up senate races are deadlocked, Mississippi was, until recently, regarded as inviolable. But Scott Colom’s campaign to unseat Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith has attracted conspicuous campaigners, including Harris, who appeared last week and Pete Buttigieg, scheduled to rally with Colom on Tuesday evening in Biloxi. 

Colom would, if elected, become Mississippi’s first African-American senator since Blanche Bruce, who served one term after being elected in 1875. No Mississippi Democrat has won a senate seat since 1982. But the party has begun to invest in Colom’s campaign, buoyed by the national resurgence in red strongholds and the hunch that Colom’s recognition as a district attorney could tap into both the state’s significant black demographic of 36 per cent and the national disillusionment at spiralling fuel and grocery prices. Still, actually winning would represent a stunning result. Sharon Peters, a staff member in Borroum’s, explains what Trump means to her after the last of the close-down chores are completed.

[ As Donald Trump weighs up options, could inflation be about to get worse?Opens in new window ]

“I look at what I grew up with – we used to be strong internationally, and among ourselves. And we hadn’t been there for many years – until this guy came along. And he is having to undo a lot of things that should have been addressed many years ago. He is not a polished politician, at all. He can be crude. But I would call it forthright. As a person it doesn’t bother me, but it is very offensive to other people. He is burning all of that to the ground.”

The late decision to add Mississippi to Trump’s daily blitz of rallies was quickly interpreted as another sign of Republican panic over the library of polling data suggesting that a catastrophic midterm night is coming down the tracks. Even so, Scott Colom trails Hyde-Smith by an average of six points in most of the polling. Mississippi remains new-Republican heartland and this county, nestled just south of Tennessee and a half-hour west of the Alabama state line, seems like alien territory for any Democratic aspirant.

[ US midterms: can Democrats take the Senate?Opens in new window ]

“Well, Mississippi is a red state,” Shane Eaten says with a shrug when I ask him why Trump is so popular here.

“Most people vote Republican here. I just don’t see how the other side, the Democrats, most people around here just don’t line up with them. This area is conservative, Christian, this whole area’s called the Bible Belt, of course.”

He has driven across from Booneville, about a half-hour west in Alabama. He’d left his mobile phone in the car and was retrieving it while his daughter stood in line. We stand on the hill beside the arena surveying the drift of people snaking hundreds of metres back in the warm afternoon. They had begun arriving at nine in the morning. For weeks, Trump’s rallies had attracted lacklustre crowds, but this scene seemed like a return to the evangelism of 2024. Nothing the Democrats have offered, Eaten says, even since the last election, has resonated with his vision for the United States.

“I feel like Trump is for America. Like he says: make America great again. I believe that. I know the war in Iran is costing us money but I believe that will be under control after the election. It may take a little while, but he will get prices down with the pipeline they just signed for. But, you know, I build houses for a living. Last time Trump was president, it was booming. Work was everywhere. When Biden got in, everything stopped. Of course, the pandemic had a lot to do with that, I do accept that. But yeah, everything got slower and it hadn’t improved a whole bunch.”

Nearby, Mary Barrett is sitting on the grass bank with her friend. They’ve persuaded family to stand in line too. She, too, is adamant the Democratic message has made absolutely no impression on her political leanings.

“I don’t want to see all the things the Democrats are putting across myself. The last 10 years almost makes you afraid of what this world is coming to. Trump stands for all the things I want to see. I want to see my grandchildren have the freedom of speech and the freedom to do what’s right. And I feel that has been curtailed. Before Biden got out, I even thought about keeping extra food in our house. I have started locking our doors – we never did that before.”

She shakes her head when asked whether she’d always been Republican.

“No, in fact my parents were Democrats. We were all Democrats, to be honest, until what they’ve gone to today – gone woke, gone anti-police, gone anti-Ice. We don’t want the foreigners here if they are not here legally. They are not like my daddy’s Democrats. And my daddy was a true, hard Democrat.”

The Republican rap against Colom, and the other Democratic contenders threatening to flip red states, is that they are the antithesis of those old values. Mississippi television adverts portray Colom as a big-donor beneficiary and align him with the transgender fearmongering that has been a central element of the Trump second-term manifesto. “They call him the transgender defender,” runs one attack advert airing on repeat. “Colom bragged: ‘you can’t run to the left of me.’ Believe him. Mississippi’s better choice: Cindy Hyde Smith for US Senate.’

But strolling through the fringes of the Trump crowd outside the Crossroads arena on Monday was Colom himself, shaking hands and speaking with people waiting to get in. Later, he would describe Trump’s impromptu visit as “a sign of our momentum and of how desperate he is. I think this is the best proof of it: the president of the United States, in Corinth, Mississippi, eight days before an election.’”

And there is something faintly surreal about the descent, over the afternoon, of secret service security lockdown on sedate rabbit runs such as Levee Road and Bell School Road around the arena. Residents stick hastily crafted parking signs, ranging from $10 to $30 on their front lawns. Neighbours stand around talking, shading their eyes as they scan the sky for any sighting of the presidential aircraft. Locals line the roadside at the cafes and petrol stations to catch the presidential cavalcade as it moves past them in a blur of blue lighting and black limousine sheen. The entire event is a diversion: no ordinary Monday evening.

[ Ted Smyth: Don’t mistake protest votes for Democrat support in US midtermsOpens in new window ]

Joe’s Shoes, on Filmore Street, looks out on to the green and the Corinth tourism office. “You can tell everyone’s already headed out there,” says Tracy Tomlinson, who is at the front desk.

“Everybody’s gotten real excited about it.”

She has already phoned Chris Latch, whose father, Joe, eventually bought the store from Joe Blankenship after starting work there at the age of 14. Latch arrives in to offer his welcomes and a quick history of the evolution of the store. “My father’s family grew up poor sharecroppers, things like that. But yeah, he worked here all his life and then he eventually bought it.”

Tomlinson jokes that they are trying to nudge Joe towards social media but the retention of the old cash register and written receipt books is part of an observance of local custom. Borroum’s offers similar touches, such as store credit and free delivery. We talk about business and how the tariff upheaval as gradually made its presence felt along Filmore Street.

“Oh yeah. We see it on a lot of our inventory,” says Latch.

“Just prices. It’s kind of like how they say you boil a frog a little bit at a time. And prices just inching up and it makes it difficult on people. So yeah, fuel, groceries – the things that people have to have.”

It’s the national complaint against which Trump has been attempting to defend himself over the course of an extraordinary midterm cycle in which he has stubbornly presented himself, in defiance of historically low personal approval ratings, as the surrogate candidate on the ballot.

By six o’clock, downtown Corinth is stunningly peaceful: the only sound to be heard near the railway crossing is of the water fountain feature. It moves to its own self-assured time and even the arrival of the sitting president, who has begun to speak in the big arena just outside town, cannot alter that rhythm.

A man in a pickup driving past the railway tracks slows down and rolls his window after seeing the camera.

“You railroaders?” he asks and then nods at the mention of the Trump rally. He tells us he couldn’t get off work to go. Like most people in Corinth, he’s effusive in his welcome.

“I hope you enjoy our town,” he calls as he pushes the truck into gear.

Twilight falls quickly and out by the arena, people who didn’t get into the event are walking back across the overpass, headed for their parked cars and home as below them, the traffic shoots by on the busy US 45 to Tupelo.
news.summary: No Democrat has won a senate seat in Mississippi since 1982 but with momentum building behind Scott Colom in advance of the midterms, the US president decided to pay a visit
news.author: Keith Duggan
