news.title: Trump's cure for Republicans' midterm woes is more Trump. Will it work?
news.text:
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump likes to play make-believe with his supporters.

“Just close your eyes,” he tells them, “and pretend I'm on the ballot.”

It's a typically self-involved appeal from someone who has been the center of the nation's political gravity for more than a decade. Now, he's finishing the midterms with a cross-country blitz of campaign rallies that allow him to bask in applause when he's otherwise profoundly unpopular. 

In a year marked by the war with Iran, fears about artificial intelligence, redistricting fights, high energy prices and increasing concerns about the cost of living, Trump's deeply personal approach might be the election cycle's biggest gamble. 

Republicans still love the president, who remains dominant even as he approaches the back half of his second term. But his approval ratings are low enough to potentially sink his party and its bid to maintain control of Congress. 

“I don’t think there’s anybody that wants Donald Trump out there at these rallies more than Democratic candidates," said Jessica Mackler, president of EMILY’s List, which focuses on electing Democratic women who support abortion rights. 

Every time there's another Trump event, she said, “we look at that as a win.”

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said Trump is “the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party.”

“The choice has never been more clear,” he said in a statement. “Doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda, or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.” 

It goes far beyond a whirlwind rally schedule. 

The president organized even small details of the first-ever Republican midterm convention last month in Dallas, speaking both nights. He also was depicted there as the Marlboro Man, a cowboy on horseback and with a white Stetson who could ride to the rescue, on everything from baseball caps to beer cozies.

Trump even has a personal spin on his blockbuster attempt to win over voters by pledging big checks if Republicans hold Congress, saying “I’ll give you $5,000” even though the improbable idea would likely need lawmaker approval. 

Political groups associated with the president have spent at least around $277 million since Sept. 1 to help Republicans — a staggering sum that nonetheless didn't completely drain the $416 million that Trump’s flagship Super PAC, MAGA Inc., had in the bank to start last month. 

But that wasn't enough for Trump. He used taxpayer funding to run television ads celebrating himself, including one nearly identical to a spot from 2024 — the last time he really was on the ballot.

From expanding executive power, to turning the presidency into a profit center for his family, to molding the White House in his own gilded image, Trump's self regard has escalated since he won back the White House.

“I can do stuff that is unbelievable," he bragged at a rally in Kentucky.

Trump crammed the Oval Office with gold flourishes, demolished the East Wing to build a sprawling ballroom and converted the Rose Garden into a patio space reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago estate. There's also a new helipad that he showed off to Xi Jinping, China's communist leader, during a recent visit. 

The president is focused on reshaping Washington as well, dispatching National Guard troops to the streets, closing the Kennedy Center after failed attempts to add his name to the building, planning a towering arch just outside the city and pushing to revamp a century-old public golf course. 

Trump has wielded his iron grip on the Republican Party in ways that could hurt its chances in some races. He helped Ken Paxton, who has a history of legal and ethical problems, defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Texas primary, making the general election campaign against Democrat James Talarico more competitive.

Trump also clashed with North Carolina Sen. Tom Tillis, prompting him to retire, and pushed Michael Whatley to run. Now Republicans are bracing to lose the seat to former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper.

The Trump-centric approach backfired during his first term in 2018, when a similar presidential rally barrage didn't stop Democrats from retaking House control. 

This time, many of the issues that helped Trump win reelection in 2024, such as his handling of the economy, could prove to be liabilities for Republicans. 

Just 17% of U.S. adults approve of Trump's handling of the cost of living, as the Iran war keeps fuel prices high and stokes inflation fears, according to an AP-NORC poll conducted in late September. 

The White House points to highlights beyond Trump's personal appeal, like efforts to lower prescription drug prices, stimulate domestic manufacturing, crack down on the U.S.-Mexico border and oppose transgender rights. 

But longtime Michigan pollster Richard Czuba said the president's decision to focus on himself has prevented Republicans from courting conservative voters disappointed in Trump. 

“He’s literally driving people who disagree with him to the Democratic side," Czuba said.

“The dividing line is how voters feel about Donald Trump,” he added. “And there’s a whole lot more voters who disapprove of Donald Trump than approve of Donald Trump.”

A CNN/SSRS poll conducted in mid-October found that about 4 in 10 registered voters suggested they’d think of their vote for Congress as more about sending a message that they oppose Trump. Only about 2 in 10 said they would be sending a message supporting him. 

Even while hopscotching the country, the president has generally stuck to reliably red states. When he goes to battlegrounds, he mostly visits conservative areas, thus ensuring especially adoring crowds. 

A pre-speech video likens the president to a global savior, booming repeatedly, “God gave us Trump," and he usually spends more of his speeches repeating past grievances than talking about next week's Election Day. 

The idea is to energize the Republican base while avoiding backlash in swing states — and also potentially reaching television viewers who see the adulation for Trump and may vote Republican elsewhere around the country. 

“I always cater to my base," Trump recently told the Washington Examiner, when asked if he was focusing too much on sympathetic rallygoers, rather than wooing independents. 

Trump’s endorsement can be enough for some. Cindy Downes, a 67-year-old retiree from North Liberty, Iowa, cast an early ballot for Rep. Ashley Hinson for U.S. Senate and Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks' reelection. 

“The number one reason: POTUS supports them,” said Downes, who wore a MAGA hat to a recent campaign event. “I trust him. I trust his judgment.”

But LuAnn Bird, 72, of Hales Corners, Wisconsin, said opposing Trump was one of many reasons she’s supporting Democrats.

“It just feels so good, not just to go against Trump, but to go for something,” said Bird, who attended a Milwaukee rally where former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris appeared with the Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley. “I want to see an aggressive, progressive agenda.”

Mackler of EMILY’S List recently spent time in states Trump has visited, including Georgia, Florida and Ohio. She said the president's approach exposes a disconnect with voters who "are so frustrated and fed up with this agenda that’s making their lives worse." 

“That’s what’s driving opportunity on the ballot,” she said, "including in states and races and places that we would not have imagined would be in play.”

Associated Press writers Scott Bauer in Milwaukee, Hannah Fingerhut in Coralville, Iowa, and Amelia Thomson DeVeaux in Washington contributed to this report.
news.summary: President Donald Trump wants midterm voters to imagine he's on the ballot and has seized the political spotlight in a way that makes such make-believe seem a bit more real
news.author: Will Weissert Associated Press

news.title: Republicans emphasize transgender ads, putting cultural issues over economy
news.text:
NEW YORK -- Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats in the final phase of this year’s midterm elections, betting that struggling GOP candidates can leverage the divisive cultural issue to overcome voters' concerns about President Donald Trump's leadership and the state of the economy. 

The massive investment through Oct. 25 produced about 217,000 TV spots nationwide and exceeds the amount Republicans spent on similar ads in 2024, a presidential election year, at the same point before Election Day, according to tallies provided to The Associated Press by data firm AdImpact.

The spending campaign matched messaging from other Republicans on the campaign trail, led by Trump, who has played down surging gasoline prices and other rising costs, but highlighted what he described as an urgent threat to America's children from Democratic policies. 

The Republican emphasis on transgender issues offers a consequential test of whether a theme that had worked in past elections — and especially in deep red states — can still be potent when voters consistently say high prices are their chief concern.

Barely five minutes into his speech during Monday night’s rally in Corinth, Mississippi, Trump said that Democrats “promote the transgender mutilization of your children.” During his Sunday rally in Florida, Trump said “men in women's sports” four times and gender “mutilization” — meaning mutilation — another four times. 

Having shifted away from abortion, few cultural issues reflect the Republican Party's evolution on social issues in the age of Trump more than transgender rights. Though a tiny number of Americans are directly affected by legislation designed to protect transgender people from discrimination, Republicans have used the issue as a powerful emotional motivator, especially in Republican-leaning states where they need to win to maintain control of Congress.

Texas’ high-stakes Senate contest alone has consumed the largest share of Republican-backed transgender-related spending, drawing an estimated $58 million for more than 50,000 airings, according to AdImpact. But the GOP is also investing heavily in related attacks against Democrats in Ohio, Kansas, South Carolina, Iowa and Mississippi, according to an AP analysis of the data.

The Republican Party's focus stands in stark contrast to what voters say they care most about this midterm season. 

“Republicans clearly believe these issues expose a cultural disconnect between Democratic candidates and a significant portion of the electorate,” said Republican pollster Chris Wilson. “It's not necessarily that transgender policy is a top voting priority, it’s that voters can use a candidate’s position on it as a proxy for their broader values and judgment.”

Only about 1 in 10 registered voters say transgender issues are “one of the most important issues” in the election, according to an AP-NORC poll from October. 

That falls well below the roughly 8 in 10 who mentioned the economy or the cost of living, and also falls short of other issues that have surfaced during the campaign, including healthcare and the war with Iran.

Republicans were more likely than independents and Democrats to say transgender issues are highly important to this election, but it still fell below other issues.

The issue resonates with voters like Jerry Casner, a 74-year-old registered Republican and three-time Trump voter, who lives in Mechanicsburg, Pennsylvania. He retired from a nearby Army depot and works 12 hours a week at a grocery store in New Cumberland.

“Well, I don’t like the way the Democrats operate," Casner said, when asked what national issues are important to him. He explained: “If you can’t even determine the difference between a man and a woman, but yet you’re going to make life and death decisions for me, oh, I don’t think so. That’s disgusting.”

Casner said he plans on voting Republican up and down the ballot.

Republicans across federal, state and local races have aired transgender-themed ads during the general election around 217,000 times at a cost estimated at $183 million through Oct. 25, AdImpact found. That's up from $151 million in spending in the 2024 general election as of the same number of days prior to that year’s election.

Democrats have spent roughly $11 million on transgender-related ads, largely to defend themselves from the attacks. 

This year's spending was concentrated in a small number of races, according to AdImpact. 

Texas PAC, the Republican super PAC largely funded by Elon Musk and supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, has at least three separate TV ads hammering Democrat James Talarico on trans issues.

One of them echoes a Trump ad from the 2024 campaign with the narrator saying that Vice President Kamala Harris is for “they, them. President Trump is for you.” The Texas ad accuses Talarico of supporting taxpayer funding of minors' sex-reassignment surgery, charging that he's “for they them, not you.”

Another Texas PAC ad claims Talarico supports taxpayer funding of gender reassignment surgery for minors, while a third accuses him of backing child abuse charges against parents who do not support transitioning their children.

“If you care about your children, do not vote for James Talarico,” the narrator says in the spot that has aired nearly 17,000 times at a cost exceeding $23 million.

In Ohio, Republican groups led by the Senate Leadership Fund PAC are running multiple trans-themed ads against Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown. 

In two of that fund's ads, someone who underwent surgery as a minor and later de-transitioned is featured describing the regret and accusing Brown of supporting such surgeries for minors. Another accuses Brown of supporting “men competing in women’s sports.”

Brown's campaign said the ads were a “total lie” and a distraction from economic issues. The independent organization PolitiFact rated the fund's ad false.

Talarico has publicly stated that he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for minors. And the attack against Brown twists a 2023 interview where Brown stated that a child’s medical decisions belong between families and doctors, not politicians.

Still, the Texas ads have aired an estimated 50,000 times overall at a cost of $58 million, representing roughly 2 in 10 ads run in the Senate race. The Ohio attacks against Brown have cost nearly $26 million.

In deeper-red states like South Carolina, which has emerged as an unlikely Senate battleground, Republicans have spent more than $5 million on transgender-themed ads. And in the Kansas Senate race, Republican transgender ads have aired 7,000 times at a cost of nearly $7 million.

“The interesting question isn’t why Republicans are running these ads, it’s whether they’re still persuading anyone or simply reinforcing attitudes voters already hold,” said Wilson, the Republican pollster. “Those are two very different things, and $100 million in spending doesn’t tell us which is happening." 

He added, "We’ll find that out on Election Day.”

Peoples reported from New York. AP writers Linley Sanders in Washington and Marc Levy in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, contributed.
news.summary: Republicans have spent an estimated $183 million on television ads focused on transgender-related attacks against Democrats in the final phase of this year’s midterm elections
news.author: Aaron Kessler Associated Press,Steve Peoples Associated Press

news.title: Trump says he's ending restrictions on climate-warming methane from oil drilling
news.text:
BILLINGS, Mont. — President Donald Trump said Tuesday that his administration is "terminating" a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.

Trump said during a campaign rally in Texas that the change would save companies and consumers billions of dollars and unlock 210 million barrels of oil. That's equivalent to about 10 days of U.S. petroleum consumption.

The move aims to encourage more domestic drilling as Trump faces criticism over high fuel prices amid the war in Iran.

Methane is responsible for about a third of planet-warming greenhouse gas emissions, scientists estimate.

Cuts in methane emissions have emerged in recent years as a global priority to slow the rate of climate change. Oil and gas operations are the largest industrial source of methane, which is the main component in natural gas and far more potent to the atmosphere than carbon dioxide in the short term.

The invisible gas leaks from equipment and is released into the atmosphere or burned off as a waste product by oil drillers.

Environmental Protection Agency Administrator Lee Zeldin previewed the changes last month, saying they would eliminate the agency's "Super Emitter Program" that requires companies to investigate and repair major methane releases from oil and natural gas facilities. The agency would also set less restrictive standards for small oil and gas wells.

Trump said during Tuesday's rally in Lubbock for Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton that Biden's plan "crushed the small operators" with crippling regulations.

"I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion in costs," Trump said.

The loosening of the emissions rule comes as Trump and Republicans in Congress have been methodically dismantling climate policies enacted under former President Joe Biden. That's included the revocation of a scientific finding that was central to U.S. action on greenhouse gas emissions, lower fuel economy standards for vehicles and a move to repeal emission restrictions for coal and natural gas power plants.

Environmental groups said the latest rollback will let companies continue polluting the atmosphere with gas that could be captured and provide energy to millions of households.

Environmental Defense Fund President Fred Krupp said it gives a "free pass" to companies at the expense of American consumers.

"EPA should be fighting this waste, not making it easier," he said.

Zeldin has said the methane rule would have cost $18 billion and was holding back the U.S. energy industry.

The Biden methane rule was announced by officials including former Vice President Kamala Harris during a 2023 U.N. climate conference in the United Arab Emirates.

Federal officials under Biden said it would prevent an estimated 58 million tons (52.6 million metric tonnes) of methane emissions by 2038 and reduce other pollutants that cause health problems.

By 2034, the rule was projected to yield $98 billion in benefits. That figure was derived by calculating the future "social costs" of greenhouse gas emissions on public health and the environment, an approach rejected by Trump's EPA.

While previous regulations focused only on new oil and gas wells in the U.S., the Biden rule regulated existing wells. Operators also would have needed to plug leaking methane from smaller wells that produce just 6% of the nation's oil and gas while accounting for up to half of all methane emissions from oil and gas fields.

The final rule was published in 2024. The EPA last year imposed an 18-month delay to give companies time to meet new inspection requirements and other provisions.

The rule was crafted to be coordinated with a methane fee, approved in the 2022 climate law. The fee program would have levied a "waste emissions charge" of as much as $1,500 per metric ton of methane on energy producers that exceed a certain level of methane emissions.

The fee marked the first time the U.S. government directly imposed a fee, or tax, on greenhouse gas emissions. Congress repealed it weeks after Trump took office.

Officials also tried to rein in methane from oil and gas under former President Barack Obama, but that effort was scaled back during Trump's first term.
news.summary: President Donald Trump said that his administration is "terminating" a Biden-era rule that aimed to cut planet-warming emissions of methane from oil and gas drilling.
news.author: The Associated Press

news.title: Why Trump Flew to Corinth: Mississippi Senate Poll Has Hyde-Smith Just Three Points Ahead of Scott Colom
news.text: Donald Trump flew to Corinth, Mississippi, on Monday, 26 October, to rally for Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. Days earlier, a poll had her just three points ahead of Democrat Scott Colom. Trump said she was doing great, then added, 'I can't take a chance,' warning that voters stay home when a candidate looks safe.That lead is within the 3.5-point margin of error, in a state Trump won by roughly 23 points in 2024. No Democrat has won a Senate seat there since 1982. The survey came from a Democratic firm, and most other measures still favour Hyde-Smith before the 3 November vote.What the Mississippi Senate Poll ShowsChange Research carried out the survey for the 365 Project on 21 and 22 October. It put Hyde-Smith on 43 per cent and Colom on 40 per cent. Ty Pinkins, the Democratic Senate nominee in 2024 who now runs as an independent, took 6 per cent. Most public polls in the race have come from firms aligned with Democrats, though Wedgewood Polls found Hyde-Smith leading 52 per cent to 48 per cent in a survey conducted on 12–14 October. Poliwave's average of two recent polls gives Hyde-Smith a 3.3-point lead.Other trackers give the senator a wider cushion. The Pollsmax average had her about seven points clear, with a 93 per cent win chance, and Kalshi, a prediction market, priced her chances near 89 per cent. Poliwave's wider forecast has her 6.8 points ahead and rates the race Likely Republican. Last week the Cook Political Report shifted its rating from Solid to Likely Republican, while Inside Elections still rates it Solid Republican.Why Republicans Are Paying AttentionTrump's standing in Mississippi has weakened. The Civiqs tracker of registered voters put his approval there at 41 per cent and his disapproval at 52 per cent on 21 October, his weakest reading in the state in either term. In 2020, Hyde-Smith won by 10 points while Trump's winning margin topped 16. Trump also held two rallies for her before her 2018 runoff against Democrat Mike Espy, which she won.Colom, a district attorney based in Columbus, gained traction after an ad attacking Hyde-Smith over beef prices went viral. If he wins, he would be Mississippi's first Black US senator since Reconstruction. National Democrats have backed him, with Kamala Harris holding a rally for Colom in Columbus on Thursday. Senate Majority PAC, a Democratic group, announced a $1.2 million (£900,000) advertising campaign. Former president Barack Obama has also endorsed him.What Each Campaign Says About the VisitColom said Hyde-Smith was scared of questions about healthcare cuts, farmers and the Epstein files, and dared the president to debate him. Hyde-Smith's campaign manager, Jake Monssen, said she gladly accepted Trump's offer to boost turnout and that voters deserved to hear directly from the president, whose explanation is in the clip below.Republican strategist Hayes Dent said the visit would probably cost Hyde-Smith three or four points but would not change the outcome. Henry Barbour, a Republican National Committee member, said a big turnout would favour Hyde-Smith. Colom's team has the resources and momentum to win, his campaign manager, Gerard Henderson, told the Associated Press.
news.author: Christian Nogot Puno
